Seed dispersal approximated an exponential decay curve (see also Janzen 1970; Okubo and Levin 1989; Willson 1992). Most seeds fell within 5 m of adults for *D*. *excelsa* and within 3 m of adults for *T*. *speciosissima* (Fig. 1).

342	
343	Burrows et al.: Post-fire juvenile period of plants in SW Australia
344	
345	burning can be planned and implemented under seasonal and diurnal weather conditions to exploit these temporal and spatial flammability differentials, thereby reducing the risk of burning fire sensitive species and communities too frequently. In south-west forest landscapes, low intensity prescribed fires set under moist conditions in spring usually burn the drier parts of the landscape, such as forested uplands, but often do not burn riparian zones and areas of sparse fine surface fuels such as rock outcrops. The proportion of the landscape that is sufficiently dry to burn increases rapidly with the onset of summer drying and where fuels are continuous, fires in summer and autumn usually burn the entire landscape.
346	
347	## Conclusion
348	
349	Juvenile period can be used as a biological indicator to help determine ecologically acceptable minimum intervals between fires in various ecosystems. The post-fire juvenile period of understorey plants in south-west forests and associated ecosystems reflects site productivity, as expressed by rainfall, and habitat flammability, as determined by seasonal moisture regime and fuel characteristics. Plants with longer juvenile periods are most likely to occur in the lower rainfall regions, and in less flammable habitats such as riparian zones, rock outcrops and some wetlands. At the landscape scale, the minimum ecologically acceptable fire interval will vary across the landscape in response to changing habitat types. In the interests of plant conservation, fire management, particularly the interval between prescribed fires, should aim to accommodate this variability.
350

25	## **Flowering, seed dispersal, seed predation and seedling recruitment in two pyrogenic flowering resprouters**
26	
27	*Andrew J*. *Denham*<sup>A</sup> *and Tony D*. *Auld*
28	
29	Biodiversity Research Group, NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service, PO Box 1967, Hurstville, NSW 2220, Australia.
30	
31	ACorresponding author; email: andrew.denham@npws.nsw.gov.au
32	
33	*Abstract.* A few resprouting plants in fire-prone environments have no local seed bank (soil or canopy) when a fire occurs. These species rely on post-fire flowering and the production of non-dormant seeds to exploit favourable post-fire establishment and growth conditions. For two such pyrogenic flowering species (*Doryanthes excelsa* Correa and *Telopea speciosissima* (Smith) R.Br.), we examined the timing of seed release, patterns of fruit production, seed dispersal, seed predation and seedling establishment following a fire in the Sydney region of southeastern Australia. Both species took some 19 months after the fire to flower and the first seeds were released 2 years after the fire. *D*. *excelsa* flowered and fruited only once after the fire. For *T*. *speciosissima*, plants also flowered at least once more in the subsequent 5 years, but produced seed in only the first three post-fire flowering years. Fruit production differed between species, with fruiting individuals of *D*. *excelsa* producing fewer infructescences, similar numbers of follicles, but many more seeds per follicle than fruiting individuals of *T*. *speciosissima*. Ultimately, *D*. *excelsa* produced approximately six times as many seeds per m2 and four times as many seeds per adult in one flowering season than *T*. *speciosissima* did after four flowering (three successful fruiting) seasons.
34	
35	Seeds were passively dispersed from fruits borne 3–4 m (*D*. *excelsa*) or 1–2 m (*T*. *speciosissima*) above the ground. Most seeds were found within 5 m (*D*. *excelsa*) or 3 m (*T*. *speciosissima*) of parent plants. The primary seed shadow of both species was a poor predictor of the distribution of seedlings, with more seedlings occurring further from the adults than expected from the distribution of seeds. Seed loss to predators was high in both species in exclusion experiments where mammals had access to clumps of seeds (77–88%). It was variable and generally lower (8–65%) in experiments where seeds were not locally clumped. However, for *T*. *speciosissima*, at one site, some 65% of seeds were lost to mammals and invertebrates in these latter experiments. At this site, these losses appeared to influence subsequent recruitment levels, as very low seedling densities were observed.
36	
37	For both species, germination of seedlings first occurred some 2.5–3 years after the passage of the fire. The percentage of seeds produced to seedlings successfully established was low in *D*. *excelsa* (2–3%) and more variable across sites and years in *T*. *speciosissima* (0–18%). Resultant post-fire seedling densities of *D*. *excelsa* (two sites) and *T*. *speciosissima* at one site were similar, but they were much lower at the *T*. *speciosissima* site that had high levels of seed predation. Both *D*. *excelsa* and *T*. *speciosissima* are amongst the slowest woody resprouting species to recruit seedlings after fire in south-eastern Australia and lag years behind species with soil or canopy seed banks.
38	
39	#### **Introduction**
40	
41	In fire-prone habitats, recruitment in plant species is frequently linked to the passage of a fire (Tyler 1995). This results from at least two main mechanisms. First, in species with soil seed banks, seed dormancy may be broken by the passage of fires (e.g. via heat, smoke, charred wood: Keeley 1991; Brown 1993; or interactions of these factors: Keith 1997; Morris 2000). Examples include many legumes (Jeffery *et al.* 1988; Auld and O'Connell 1991) and nonleguminous species (Brown 1993; Dixon *et al.* 1995). Second, in species with canopy seed banks, fires result in the mass opening of fruits and the release of seeds (Bond *et al.* 1984; Lamont *et al.* 1991).
42	
43	However, a number of species have no available seed storage in either the soil or canopy at the time of the passage of a fire (Keith 1996). A few may rely on dispersal from unburnt areas, but most have mechanisms that allow established plants to survive fire via buried lignotubers, rhizomes or buds (protected meristems). These species usually flower soon after fire and then release seeds (Gill 1981; Frost 1984; Johnson *et al.* 1994; Bond and van Wilgen 1996; Carrington 1999). For species dependant on post-fire flowering for recruitment (pyrogenic flowering resprouters), 
44	
45	{2}<!-- PAGE BREAK -->
46	
47	the timing and magnitude of this flowering will influence opportunities for post-fire seedling establishment. The longer the interval between the passage of a fire and seedling recruitment, the more of the available resources such as light, nutrients and space, are likely to have been captured by other resprouting species or by those species with soil or canopy seed banks that can recruit in the immediate post-fire period.
48	
49	Many individuals of pyrogenic flowering resprouting species in south-eastern Australia appear to have a single post-fire flowering (e.g. *Angophora hispida*, Auld 1986; *Blandfordia nobilis*, Johnson *et al.* 1994; *Lomatia silaifolia*, Denham and Whelan 2000; *Xanthorrhoea australis*, Gill and Ingwersen 1976, but see; *X*. *fulva*, Taylor *et al.* 1998). In such cases, this represents the only opportunity for recruitment between fires. For other species, flowering may extend over several years following a fire (e.g. *T*. *speciosissima*, Pyke 1983; Bradstock 1995; Goldingay 2000; *Xanthorrhoea australis*, Curtis 1998). However, the timing of recruitment in pyrogenic flowering resprouting species has been little studied and the degree to which each post-fire flowering event contributes to recruitment is unexplored.
50	
51	In the post-fire environment, the impact of seed predation may be reduced due to lower predator abundance and also via predator satiation, in the case of serotinous seed release (Whelan 1995; Bond and van Wilgen 1996; Myerscough *et al.* 2000). However, the seeds of pyrogenic flowering resprouters are likely to be released after most seeds from serotinous species have germinated and, consequently, would not benefit from any predator satiation effects from serotinous seed release. In addition, populations of predators may have recovered by this time. All pyrogenic flowering resprouters are thought to release seeds in a non-dormant state (Bell *et al.* 1993; Bond and van Wilgen 1996) and hence form transient soil seed banks (*sensu* Parker and Kelly 1989).
52	
53	In this study, we assessed post-fire reproduction and the patterns of seedling recruitment after a wildfire in 1994, in two resprouting species reliant on post-fire flowering for seed production (*Doryanthes excelsa* and *Telopea speciosissima*), from the Sydney area of south-eastern Australia. We examined (i) the timing of flowering and magnitude of seed production over 5 years after the fire; (ii) the pattern of seed and seedling dispersal; (iii) the level of post-dispersal seed predation; and (iv) the proportion of seeds released that resulted in successful establishment of new plants.
54	
55	#### **Methods**
56	
57	#### *Study species*
58	
59	*Doryanthes excelsa* Correa (Gymea lily—Doryanthaceae) is a large perennial rosette plant with a bulbous rhizome and long broad linear leaves up to 3 m long. It is apparently capable of asexual reproduction by branching of the rhizome (Nash 1996). It grows in dry sclerophyll forests and woodlands on soils derived from sandstone containing some clay and is restricted to the Sydney Basin in south-eastern Australia, with three outlying populations in northern New South Wales (Harden 1990–1993). The species survives fire by having apical buds protected in underground leaf bases. It flowers in a large, red inflorescence held up to 5 m above the foliage of the plant (Harden 1990–1993). Fire appears to stimulate flowering, although sporadic flowering does occur in the absence of fire (Nash 1996). The mechanism determining flowering is unknown (Beeh 1996; Nash 1996).
60	
61	*Telopea speciosissima* (Smith) R.Br. (waratah—Proteaceae) is a tall shrub, generally 2–4 m, which is also known for its striking red blooms that emerge above the resprouting shrubby vegetation in the post-fire environment. It is common in dry sclerophyll forest and woodlands on the central coast and central and southern tablelands of New South Wales (Harden 1990–1993). The species survives fire by having dormant buds protected in an underground lignotuber (Bradstock 1995). Aerial stems are completely regrown after each fire.
62	
63	#### *Sites*
64	
65	Three sample sites within a 10-km radius were chosen in Royal National Park, about 35 km south of Sydney (34°03′S, 151°03′E). All sites occurred on soils derived from the Triassic Hawkesbury Sandstone Formation, although Site 1 (with an ironstone influence) and Site 2 (with an alluvial influence) were on soils slightly more fertile than Site 3. At Site 1, both study species occurred in ironstone woodland vegetation (D. Keith and M. Tozer, unpubl. data), with an overstorey of *Eucalyptus sieberi*, *Corymbia gummifera*, *Banksia serrata*, *Xylomelum pyriforme* and *Ceratopetalum gummiferum*. The shrubby understorey included *Grevillea diffusa*, *Banksia spinulosa*, *Lissanthe strigosa*, *Prostanthera* sp., *Isopogon anemonifolius*, *Acacia myrtifolia*, *Xanthorrhoea media*, *Lomandra* spp. and *Dianella* sp. The vegetation at Site 2 (*D*. *excelsa* only) is Sandstone Gully Forest (D. Keith and M. Tozer, unpubl. data), with an overstorey of *Angophora costata*, *Banksia serrata*, *Ceratopetalum gummiferum*, *Eucalyptus piperita* and *E*. *sieberi* and a shrubby understorey that included *Boronia pinnata*, *Grevillea mucronulata*, *Acacia terminalis*, *Lomandra longifolia* and *Caustis flexuosa*. At Site 3 (*T*. *speciosissima* only) the vegetation is Sandstone Heath (D. Keith and M. Tozer, unpubl. data), with a short overstorey of *Corymbia gummifera*, *Eucalyptus obstans*, *E*. *sclerophylla* and *Banksia serrata* and a shrubby understorey that included *Lambertia formosa*, *Lissanthe strigosa* and sedges including *Xanthorrhoea media*, *Restio dimorpha* and *Cyathochaeta diandra*. Plant nomenclature follows Harden (1990–1993).
66	
67	All sites were burnt in January 1994. Before 1994, there was variation in fire history across sites. The eastern part of Site 1 (sampled for *D*. *excelsa*) and Site 3 were burnt in 1988. The western part of Site 1, separated by a road from the eastern part (sampled for both study species), and Site 2 were burnt in the early 1980s (NPWS fire records; D. Keith, pers. comm.).
68	
69	#### *Timing of flowering and seed release*
70	
71	The three study sites were monitored to observe flowering after the January 1994 fire for both species up until December 2000. As both *D*. *excelsa* and *T*. *speciosissima* flower in July–October, this involved seven potential flowering seasons (1994–2000). General observations were also made throughout Royal National Park to determine whether the pattern of the study sites was representative of the general response of the study species to fire in this area. The timing of fruit development and seed release was recorded for the first four flowering seasons after the 1994 fire.
72	
73	#### *Estimates of seed production and seedling establishment*
74	
75	Six 30 × 30-m plots were established as follows: *D*. *excelsa*, two plots at each of Sites 1 and 2; *T*. *speciosissima*, one plot at each of Sites 1 and 3. For both study species, within each plot at each site, the numbers of infructescences and follicles on all plants were scored each year (1994–2000). To estimate the number of seeds per follicle, intact
76	
77	{3}<!-- PAGE BREAK -->
78	
79	follicles were collected in autumn 1996, prior to dehiscence, for each species from each site. For *T*. *speciosissima*, samples of 23 and 25 follicles were collected from Sites 1 and 3, respectively, while for *D*. *excelsa*, samples of 15 and 29 follicles were collected from Sites 1 and 2, respectively. Seeds within these follicles were scored after dehiscence in the laboratory. For *T*. *speciosissima*, only those seeds judged as 'filled' (i.e. likely to be viable) were included in this assessment (see also Bradstock 1995; Denham and Whelan 2000). For *D*. *excelsa*, no assessment was made, although Nash (1996) found that the average viability of seeds collected from a number of locations (not including Royal National Park) was 86% (±6.2 s.e.). The individuals used to estimate numbers of seeds per follicle were sampled from outside the plots to avoid impacts on primary seed dispersal and seedling recruitment. The density of seeds per plot was estimated by multiplying the number of intact follicles by the estimate of the mean number of seeds per follicle and dividing this value by the area of each plot (900 m2 ).
80	
81	To estimate the magnitude of post-fire seedling recruitment for both study species, five randomly allocated transects each 1 × 30 m were searched for seedlings in spring 1998, within each of the 30 × 30-m plots. For *T*. *speciosissima*, we assessed the probable fruiting year from which seedlings were established, by comparisons with other seedlings of known age within the sites.
82	
83	#### *Primary seed dispersal*
84	
85	The seeds of *D*. *excelsa* are disc-like, about 15 mm in diameter, 2 mm thick, have a dry spongy texture and weigh approximately 43 mg (Westoby *et al.* 1990; Nash 1996; A. J. Denham, pers. obs.). The seeds of *T*. *speciosissima* are winged and weigh approximately 72 mg (Westoby *et al.* 1990). Westoby *et al.* (1990) considered *T*. *speciosissima* to be adapted for wind dispersal, but could only suggest that the spongy texture of *D*. *excelsa* seed could serve for wind or water dispersal. Initial seed fall from dehisced follicles in both species is passive and movement in the air appears likely to be the main means of dispersal away from the infructescence.
86	
87	The spatial pattern of initial seed fall was estimated by counting seeds found on the ground in four orthogonal transects along compass bearings from each of five isolated plants at Site 1 for *D*. *excelsa* and Sites 1 and 3 for *T*. *speciosissima*. Because of time constraints, this was not done at Site 2 for *D*. *excelsa*. Searches were done in June–August of 1996, when most seeds had fallen from the follicles. Some further redistribution of seeds along the soil surface by wind and rain after this time is likely (Lamont *et al.* 1993; Hammill *et al.* 1998). The transects for *D*. *excelsa* started approximately 0.25 m from the centre of each clump, because of the space occupied by the leaf bases of the plants. Counts of numbers of seeds were made every 0.1 m along each transect. Transects were 0.5 m wide and limited to 7.25 m long as there were no seeds seen in initial searches beyond 7.15 m. For *T*. *speciosissima*, the area occupied by the stems was included in the transects. In preliminary searches around *T*. *speciosissima* adults, no seeds were found more than 3 m from adults at Site 1 and 2 m from adults at Site 3, so the transect lengths were reduced to 3.5 and 2.5 m, respectively.
88	
89	#### *Seed predation*
90	
91	The fates of recently released seeds on the ground were examined during the initial seed release after the 1994 fire (i.e. in 1996), in two trials. First, an exclusion experiment was used to investigate the agents responsible for and the degree of post-dispersal predation at each site. It was assumed that no secondary dispersal of seeds by invertebrates such as ants was likely, since neither species have lipid bodies attached to their seeds. Westoby *et al.* (1990) suggested that neither species is myrmecochorous and field observations supported this. A block design was used with two treatments and 10 seeds per treatment per block. This experiment was set up for *D*. *excelsa* at Sites 1 and 2 and for *T*. *speciosissima* at Sites 1 and 3 as follows:
92	
93	(a) caged: cages (15 × 15 cm × 5 cm high with 1-cm<sup>2</sup> mesh size) were used to exclude vertebrate predators, while still allowing access to most invertebrates. To prevent seeds from washing away in heavy rain, a PVC ring sawn from pipe 10 cm in diameter and about 1 cm tall was placed on the ground. This ring was pushed into the soil leaving only the top 0.5 cm protruding. The cage was placed over the ring and fastened down with wire stakes.
94	
95	(b) uncaged: where only the PVC ring was used. This allowed access to both invertebrates and vertebrates.
96	
97	Ten blocks consisting of a caged and an uncaged treatment, were used for each species, at each site. The blocks were placed about 5 m apart along a transect through the site, with separate transects for each species at Site 1.
98	
99	The number of seeds remaining in each treatment block was recorded every day for the first week and approximately every second day for the following 10 weeks. Additionally, any information concerning the condition of seeds (such as whether chewed or germinated) or the presence of testa remains was recorded at each visit.
100	
101	Second, for both study species, a trial was established to examine the level of predation on seeds that were placed singly at random locations throughout the plots, rather than clumped as above (see Auld and Denham 1999, 2001). These trials were established for *D*. *excelsa* in two plots at Site 1 and in one plot at Site 2 and for *T*. *speciosissima* in one plot at each of Sites 1 and 3. A single seed was placed at each of 10 randomly located positions according to the 30 × 30-m grid established at each site, with the location marked by a steel stake 0.2 m away. Additional batches of 10 seeds were similarly placed in new random locations each week for the following 3 weeks. The fate of these seeds was followed for the next 10 weeks, with details recorded as for the exclusion experiment. Only 'filled' seeds were used in these experiments.
102	
103	#### *Seedling dispersal*
104	
105	The following two different estimates were made of the dispersal pattern of seedlings around adult plants:
106	
107	(a) the ground was searched for seedlings up to a distance of 10 m from fruiting plants around five isolated plants of *D*. *excelsa* at Site 1. The distance of each seedling from the centre of the adult was measured. The adults included two of those used to sample primary seed dispersal. Sufficient seedlings were not available at the other three adults sampled for primary seed dispersal. For *T*. *speciosissima*, this technique was not used as adults continued to flower after the first year.
108	
109	(b) for *D*. *excelsa* at Sites 1 and 2 and *T*. *speciosissima* at Sites 1 and 3, the distance of each seedling from the centre of the nearest parent was measured for all seedlings observed in the transects used for estimating seedling establishment (above). Because of the overall low number of seedlings observed for *T*. *speciosissima* at Site 3, the entire 30 × 30-m plot was surveyed. This estimate included overlapping seed shadows from adult plants, as typically occurs in the field.
110	
111	#### *Analyses*
112	
113	To test the hypothesis that fruit and seed production varied across sites and years within the study area, estimates of infructescence and follicle production per fruiting plant were compared in *D*. *excelsa* by a nested 2-factor ANOVA with plots nested within sites and in *T*. *speciosissima* across sites and years when fruit was produced, by a 2-factor ANOVA without replication. Estimates of seed production per m2 were compared in *D*. *excelsa* across sites by a 1-factor ANOVA with plots as replicates and in *T*. *speciosissima* across sites and fruiting years by a 2-factor ANOVA without replication (Zar 1996).
114	
115	To test the hypothesis that vertebrate seed predators had an impact on the number of seeds available for germination (the seed predation 
116	
117	{4}<!-- PAGE BREAK -->
118	
119	exclusion experiment), the proportions of seeds remaining in each replicate treatment within the 10 blocks after 75 days were compared by a 3-factor ANOVA (factors were treatment, site and block, with blocks nested within sites) for each species separately. The hypothesis that the two species suffered different levels of predation at Site 1, where both *D*. *excelsa* and *T*. *speciosissima* were sampled, was tested by a 3-factor ANOVA with species and caging treatment (with blocks nested within species) as factors.
120	
121	At lower seed densities than in the seed predation exclusion experiment (the single seeds trial) we tested the hypothesis that predation varied across sites. For *T*. *speciosissima*, the proportions of seeds remaining in each weekly cohort of 10 seeds at the end of the study (after 9 weeks) were compared across sites by a 1-factor ANOVA. Data for *D*. *excelsa* were similarly analysed, using both plots at Site 1 and the single plot at Site 2 as three levels in a 'location' factor. Again, it was possible to test the hypothesis that the two species suffered different levels of predation at Site 1 at this lower seed density. Here, only the western of the two *D*. *excelsa* plots was used, as it was adjacent to the *T*. *speciosissima* plot (1-factor ANOVA).
122	
123	We tested the hypothesis that seedling establishment varied across sites in both species and across years for *T*. *speciosissima*. In *D*. *excelsa*, the number of seedlings per transect was compared across sites by a nested 2-factor ANOVA with plots nested in sites. For *T*. *speciosissima*, the number of seedlings per transect was compared across sites and fruiting year of origin by a 2-factor ANOVA.
124	
125	For each ANOVA, homogeneity of variances was tested by Cochran's test. Where variances were significantly heterogeneous an arcsine transformation was applied to proportion data and a square-root transformation was applied to count data. If variances were still heterogeneous, the analysis was carried out on the raw data with a conservative approach to rejection of the null hypothesis (Underwood 1981).
126	
127	To test the hypothesis that the distributions of seedlings around plants were the same as the distributions of seeds around plants, a number of Kolmogorov–Smirnov goodness-of-fit tests were done.
128	
129	(i) For *D*. *excelsa* at Site 1, seed and seedling data from the isolated plants were placed into 0.1-m classes and frequency counts of seeds or seedlings were obtained from each distance class for all five individuals. The proportions of seeds or seedlings per distance class were then determined. Seedling data for distances less than 0.25 m from the adult were omitted, since data for seed distribution were not obtained at this distance, due to the occupation of most of the available space by the parent plants. Similarly, seedling distances greater than 7.15 m were omitted since this was distance of the furthest observed seed. A Kolmogorov–Smirnov test was used to determine the goodnessof-fit of the seedling distribution (observed) with the seed distribution (predicted) (Zar 1996).
130	
131	(ii) For *D*. *excelsa* at Site 1 and *T*. *speciosissima* at Sites 1 and 3, estimations were made of the goodness-of-fit of the seedling distributions from the plot transect sampling (observed) with the seed distributions from the isolated individuals (expected). Restriction of seedling data to the greatest distance observed for seeds (7.15 m) was as above for *D*. *excelsa*, and to 3.75 m for *T*. *speciosissima*. There was no restriction on the least distance for *T*. *speciosissima*. This test enabled the determination of whether the distribution of seeds around isolated adults adequately explained the distribution of seedlings around adults that were contagiously distributed (a more typical situation) and thus had overlapping seed shadows.
132	
133	(iii) For *D*. *excelsa* at Site 1, the seedling distribution from the five isolated plants ('expected') was compared with that obtained from the plot transect sampling ('observed'). This test assessed how well the distribution of seedlings around isolated plants of *D*. *excelsa* represented the more typical situation of contagiously distributed individuals.
134	
135	#### **Results**
136	
137	#### *Timing of flowering and seed release*
138	
139	For both *D*. *excelsa* and *T*. *speciosissima*, the first flowering after the January 1994 fires occurred in late winter (August) of 1995, some 19 months after the January 1994 fire. This pattern was found at all study sites and more generally across Royal National Park. Fruits matured in the following autumn (March–June 1996), with *D*. *excelsa* first releasing seeds in March 1996 and *T*. *speciosissima* in April 1996. Consequently, seeds were not released into the post-fire habitat until some 25–26 months after the passage of the January 1994 fire. Seed fall was quite prolonged with some seeds still in fruits in June (both species). *D. excelsa* plants in the study plots did not flower in any of the subsequent 5 years, while most *T*. *speciosissima* individuals flowered again the following year and a few in three of the subsequent 4 years (Table 1), with a similar timing of flowering and fruiting to that observed in 1995–1996.
140	
141	#### *Fruit and seed production*
142	
143	In *D*. *excelsa*, the number, and hence density, of flowering plants varied considerably between plots within sites, ranging from six at Site 1, plot 1 (0.2 m–2) to 39 at Site 2, plot 2 (1.3 m–2) (Table 1). There were no significant differences between sites in the mean numbers of infructescences (*F*1,2 = 0.86, *P* = 0.45) or follicles (*F*1,2 = 9.94, *P* = 0.09) produced per fruiting plant, although there were almost twice as many follicles produced at Site 1, plot 1, than at Site 2, plot 2 (Table 1). For *T*. *speciosissima*, the total number of individuals that flowered between 1995 and 2000 varied from 14 at Site 1 to 24 at Site 3 (Table 1). There was no significant difference in the mean number of infructescences (*F*1,2 = 0.4, *P* = 0.59) or follicles (*F*1,2 = 0.003, *P* = 0.96) per fruiting plant between sites across the 1995–1997 flowering seasons. *D. excelsa* had greater seed production per follicle than *T*. *speciosissima* (104, 105 *v.* 11 seeds per follicle, respectively, Table 2). There were no significant differences in the number of seeds per follicle between sites for *T*. *speciosissima* (*F*1,46 = 0.43, *P* = 0.52) or *D*. *excelsa* (*F*1,42 = 0.08, *P* = 0.93) (Table 2). The estimated density of seeds produced by *D*. *excelsa* varied greatly, although not significantly (*F*1,2 = 4.76, *P* = 0.16) across sites, with Site 1 producing 9.9 (±0.4 s.e.) seeds per m<sup>2</sup> and Site 2 producing 17.7 (±3.6 s.e.) (Table 3). In all cases, a greater proportion of seedlings occurred further from the adult than suggested by the seed distributions. When the distribution of seeds was compared with that of seedlings around isolated individuals of *D*. *excelsa* at Site 1, there was a difference in the shape of the respective distributions, with the distribution of seedlings fairly uniform up to about 7 m from an adult (Fig. 4). In contrast to the distribution of seeds (Fig. 1*a*), there was not a large proportion of seedlings near adults. These data suggest that seedlings had a similar likelihood of occurring anywhere up to 7 m from their parent. Where there were overlapping seed shadows from parent plants in *D*. *excelsa*, the distribution of seedlings (Fig. 5*a*) was uneven, but more or less uniform in density up to 4 m from a parent plant, with a decline further away. For *T*. *speciosissima*, the overall shape of the distributions of seeds and seedlings was similar, despite the significant difference in the distributions. The greatest proportion of seedlings occurred further from the adult than for seeds and the tail extended further from the adult (Figs 1*b*, 5*b*). The maximum difference in distributions tended to occur within 2 m from adults, suggesting that there is some interaction between adults and seedling recruitment that leads to reduced recruitment less than 2 m from adults. This effect appeared to be most pronounced in *T*. *speciosissima* at Site 1. In both species, recruits were located well beyond the limit of seeds detected in the seed-distribution surveys, suggesting either occasional long-distance dispersal directly from the infructescence or later (i.e. after our survey) dispersal occurring at ground level (Harper 1977; Hammill *et al.* 1998). 220 221 #### **Discussion** 222 223 Both pyrogenic flowering, resprouting species took some 19 months to flower after the January 1994 fire. 1	Canopy Seed Bank Dynamics and Optimum Fire Regime for the Highly Serotinous Shrub, Banksia Hookeriana
2	Author(s): N. J. Enright, Byron B. Lamont and Ralf Marsula
3	Source: Journal of Ecology, Vol. 84, No. 1 (Feb., 1996), pp. 9-17
4	Published by: British Ecological Society
5	Stable URL: http://www.jstor.org/stable/2261695
6	Accessed: 07-05-2016 01:46 UTC
7	
8	Your use of the JSTOR archive indicates your acceptance of the Terms & Conditions of Use, available at http://about.jstor.org/terms

We use information technology and tools to increase productivity and facilitate new forms of scholarship. For more information about JSTOR, please contact support@jstor.org.

12	Wiley, British Ecological Society are collaborating with JSTOR to digitize, preserve and extend access to Journal of Ecology
13	
14	<!-- PAGE BREAK -->
15	
16	*Journal of Ecology* 1996, **84**, 9-17
17	
18	# Canopy seed bank dynamics and optimum fire regime for the highly serotinous shrub, *Banksia hookeriana*
19	
20	N.J. ENRIGHT,\*† BYRON B. LAMONT† and RALF MARSULA‡
21	
22	\*Department of Geography and Environmental Studies, University of Melbourne, Parkville, 3052, Australia, †School of Environmental Biology, Curtin University of Technology, GPO Box U1987 Perth, 6001, Australia and ‡Sektion Ökosystemanalyse, UFZ-Umweltforschungszentrum, Leipzig-Halle GmbH, Permoserstr. 15, PF 2, O-7050 Leipzig, Germany
23	
24	## Summary
25	
26	1 *Banksia hookeriana* is a serotinous nonsprouting shrub restricted to the fire-prone northern sandplain scrub-heaths of Western Australia. Evidence of the natural fire frequency to which the species is best adapted was sought through analysis of its seed demography using a computer model of canopy seed bank dynamics based on field data.
27	
28	2 Plants began flowering at 3-4 years of age but storage of viable seeds in the canopy was rare for plants < 5 years. Infructescences (cones) contained a mean of 12 follicles, holding two seeds of which 62% were estimated to be viable.
29	
30	3 Cone (and seed) production increased with plant age to 15 years, but then fluctuated widely around a mean of 17 cones per year. By this time the average plant had an estimated canopy seed bank of 700 viable seeds comprising seeds 1–10 years old.
31	
32	4 Seeds were lost from the canopy seed bank through spontaneous follicle rupture (i.e. in the absence of fire), granivory by insect larvae, and decay. Most follicles remained closed for at least 5 years and up to 50% of follicles were still closed after 10 years. Insect granivores destroyed 18% of seeds in 1-year-old cones, and continued to destroy seeds in older cones at a rate of 2-3% per year.
33	
34	5 The seed bank model predicted continued seed accumulation in the canopy to at least age 25 years (1400 seeds), but by this time more viable seeds (~ 2200) had been lost to spontaneous opening, granivory and decay than were then stored on the plant.
35	
36	6 Shannon–Weiner diversity (H′) of seed ages in the canopy seed bank increased with plant age, while evenness (V′) decreased at first (to plant age 17 years) and then increased.
37	
38	7 On a time-scale of many generations, the likelihood of successful recruitment of individuals in the next generation (on average), occurs for a fire frequency of 15-18 years. At this frequency resource wastage in this low-nutrient environment would be minimized.
39	
40	8 Recent fires have recurred within 7-11 years and indicate a human impact on the natural fire regime which may ultimately threaten the species.
41	
42	*Keywords*: *Banksia*, fire frequency, seed bank model, seed demography, serotiny
43	
44	*Journal of Ecology* (1996) **84**, 9-17
45	
46	## Introduction
47	
48	Serotiny refers to the retention of seeds in closed fruits within the plant canopy for more than one year, and can be contrasted with two alternative fates of seeds: storage in a soil seed bank, or release of short-lived seeds upon maturity (no seed storage) (Lamont *et al.* 1991a). Seed release in serotinous species is normally triggered by fire and seeds are short-lived after release, germinating during the first favourable period (Cowling & Lamont 1987). Species can range from weakly serotinous, where most seeds are released within a few years of production, to strongly serotinous, where seeds are held in the canopy for many years. The
49	
50	Correspondence: Dr Neal Enright, Department of Geography and Environmental Studies, University of Melbourne, Parkville, 3052, Australia, Fax: 61 393444972, E-mail: Enright@ariel.ucs.unimelb.edu.au
51	
52	© 1996 British Ecological Society
53	
54	<!-- PAGE BREAK -->
55	
56	10 Canopy seed bank dynamics in *Banksia hookeriana*
57	
58	ecological significance of serotiny seems clear: where conditions for seedling recruitment are best immediately following fire (i.e. competition for light, moisture and nutrients are probably at their minimum), cued release of canopy-stored seeds after fire maximizes the age, and therefore canopy seed store, of the population by the time of the next fire. Any seedlings that establish later during the interfire period have a low probability of survival due to competition with their parents and other established plants (Cowling & Lamont 1987; Lamont & Barker 1988). They will be much younger and, on average, will have a smaller canopy seed bank when fire recurs and so are less fit (*sensu* Stearns 1992).
59	
60	The dynamics of seed production, storage and loss in relation to plant age determines the range of fire frequencies for which population maintenance is possible. If fire occurs either before the onset of reproductive maturity, or before a sufficient canopy seed bank has accumulated, then a population is threatened with extinction.
61	
62	In the absence of fire some seeds are released by the spontaneous opening of old fruits, but the likelihood of plant recruitment and survival to reproductive age is extremely low. Seed release is hastened by the death of stem tissue due to drought stress and plant senescence (Witkowski *et al.* 1991). This means that the canopy seed bank may be completely lost where plant death occurs before the next fire, a fate not shared by most soil seed bank species where seeds may survive for many years after the death of parent plants (Baker 1989). Because dry plant biomass is more readily consumed by fire, any seeds held in the canopy of dead plants at the time of fire are also likely to perish (Lamont & Barker 1988).
63	
64	*Banksia hookeriana* Meissn. (Proteaceae) is a highly serotinous, fire-killed (nonsprouting) woody shrub to 2.5 m high which is restricted to the northern sandplain scrub-heaths of south-western Australia about 250-330 km north of Perth (George 1981; Taylor & Hopper 1988). Seeds are held in a state of enforced dormancy within woody follicles on large infructescences (cones) in the crown. While new inflorescences may be damaged and removed from plants by birds, mature cones normally remain attached to the plant throughout its life. Some seeds abort during development, while others are either released gradually or (especially after fire) are consumed by insects, lose viability and decay, or remain viable. Once released seeds germinate with the onset of winter rains or perish as there is no persistent soil seed bank (Enright & Lamont 1989).
65	
66	The geographical extent (80 × 30 km) of the low nutrient, noncalcareous, sandplain defines the distribution of this species, which is further limited by its specific preference for the deeper sands of low dune crests (Enright & Lamont 1989; Lamont *et al.* 1989). This means that the species exists as a large number of discrete populations of varying sizes (< 100 to > 10 000 individuals) separated by distances of 0.2 to > 1 km. The largest populations are located near Mt Adams in the northern part of the species range. Land clearance for agriculture, mining and mineral exploration, and increased incidence of anthropogenic ignition, make habitat loss and increased fire frequency potential threats to the long term survival of this species. In addition, its attractive orange inflorescences are harvested in large numbers for the commercial wildflower trade, so reducing seed production in exploited populations (Witkowski *et al.* 1994).
67	
68	This paper describes seed production and availability, and a computer model of seed bank dynamics in *Banksia hookeriana* in relation to plant age (= time since last fire) for sites near Mt Adams. The following questions were posed:
69	
70	1 What is the pattern of seed production with plant age, and what factors influence the rate of seed accumulation in the crown (e.g. level of serotiny, granivory, seed abortion and longevity)?
71	
72	2 Does the analysis of seed demography reveal the optimum fire frequency to which the species is adapted, and the range of fire frequencies compatible with population survival?
73	
74	### STUDY AREA
75	
76	The study was located in the Yardanogo Nature Reserve about 330 km north of Perth (29°25′S, 114°58′E). Mean annual rainfall at the two closest climate stations is 513 mm (Eneabba; 55 km to the south) and 471 mm (Dongara; 25 km to the north), respectively. There is a pronounced winter maximum with almost no rain (median 20 mm) in the five summer months from December to April. Temperature regimes are similar for both climate stations: mean maximum temperature in the hottest month (January) is 35.8 °C, mean minimum temperature in the coolest month (July) is 9.2 °C. Soils vary from acidic, leached sands on low dunes to sandy clays in intervening depressions (Hnatiuk & Hopkins 1981). The vegetation of the low dunes is a diverse scrub-heath usually dominated by two *Banksia* species, *Banksia hookeriana* and *Banksia attenuata* R. Br., although up to six banksias may co-occur (Beard 1984; Enright & Lamont 1989).
77	
78	## Materials and methods
79	
80	Seven sample plots, each 400 m² in area and ranging in age since last fire from 1 to 3 and 14-16 years, were established in 1986 and monitored for 6-8 years. They were on the crests and slopes of low, sandy dunes in scrub-heath along the edge of a 2-km section of Mt Adams Road within the Yardanogo Nature Reserve. Sites covering a broader range of *Banksia hookeriana* stand ages could not be located.
81	
82	© 1996 British Ecological Society, *Journal of Ecology*, **84**, 9-17
83	
84	<!-- PAGE BREAK -->
85	
86	11 N.J. Enright *et al.*
87	
88	For the five plots where plant age was 1-3 years at the start of the study, and when fire occurred subsequently during the study period (wildfire killed all plants in four of these five plots in 1991), age at time of last fire was estimated for 10 plants by the stem node ageing method described by Lamont (1985), or was known precisely. Seed production was estimated by counting the total number of cones on a random sample of 10 plants and the number of follicles on each of 10 randomly chosen cones per plant. The onset and level of flower head (inflorescence) and cone (infructescence) production were recorded within five replicate 25-m² subplots per plot for each year until 1991 (four plots) or 1993 (one plot).
89	
90	For the two plots where plant age was 14-16 years in 1986, the total number of plants and total number of cones per plant was determined. For a random sample of 10 plants per plot, the height and crown diameter, and number of new cones was enumerated each year there-after until 1991 (when wildfire killed all plants in one plot) or 1993. Plots were searched each year for evidence of seedling establishment from spontaneous release of seeds in the absence of fire.
91	
92	Complete cone crops were harvested from 10 randomly chosen 16-year-old plants at the start of the study in 1986. Cones were allocated to annual age classes using the stem node ageing method so that the entire history of reproduction could be determined for each plant. Degree of serotiny was based on the proportion of follicles per cone age class which had opened in the absence of fire (Cowling & Lamont 1985a). Cones were burned and subjected to wet-dry cycles to induce follicle rupture and facilitate seed removal (Cowling & Lamont 1985b). The numbers of follicles, and proportions of firm, aborted, eaten and decayed seeds were determined per plant by cone age. Viability of firm seeds was assessed by germinating batches of 25 seeds per cone age class from each of five plants (replicates) under moist conditions at 15 °C (Cowling *et al.* 1987).
93	
94	### STATISTICAL ANALYSES
95	
96	Trends between seed parameters, plant age and cone age were analysed using regression models (SYSTAT 1992). Where data were not normally distributed, logarithmic (ln) and arcsine transformations were employed to satisfy assumptions of the regression models used. All error terms listed are standard errors.
97	
98	A canopy seed bank dynamics model, written in programming language C++, was used to estimate the pattern of viable seed retention on plants and fate of seeds in relation to age. The model used regression equations and other statistics relating patterns of seed accumulation and loss to increasing plant and cone age. Shannon–Weiner diversity (H′) and evenness (V′) were calculated for the distribution of viable seed ages by plant age.
99	
100	## Results
101	
102	### CONE PRODUCTION
103	
104	A few plants produced inflorescences at 3-4 years of age, but these were all sterile (age 3: mean inflorescences per plant = 0.12 ± 0.06; age 4: mean = 0.92 ± 0.23). Plants first produced fertile cones at an age of 5 years. Cone production increased until plants were about 15 years old, after which annual production fluctuated widely about an average of 17 cones per year (Fig. 1a; Table 1). Both within and between year variability in cone production per plant increased with plant age.
105	
106	The total number of cones held in the crown increased continuously with plant age and although the standard error also increased with age, the mean pattern of accumulation showed a consistent trend (Fig. 1b, Table 1).
107	
108	### SEED PRODUCTION
109	
110	Cones of *Banksia hookeriana* contained up to 20 woody follicles, each of which held two seeds. The maximum possible number of seeds on a plant can
111	
112	[Graphs: (a) NO. OF CONES PER YEAR (0-40) and (b) TOTAL NO. OF CONES ON PLANT (0-200) against PLANT AGE (Y), 0-25]
113	
114	**Fig. 1** (a) The number of cones produced per year in relation to plant age, and (b) the total number of cones held in the crown in relation to plant age for *Banksia hookeriana* near Mt Adams, Western Australia. Note: standard errors are calculated for the 10 plants which were aged and harvested at the start of the study in 1986, and subsequently for total cones on random sets of 10 plants each year to 1993.
115	
116	<!-- PAGE BREAK -->
117	
118	12 Canopy seed bank dynamics in *Banksia hookeriana*
119	
120	**Table 1** Equations describing the pattern of seed accumulation and loss in relation to plant and cone age (as numbered in Fig. 3) for *Banksia hookeriana* near Mt Adams, Western Australia. Parameters related to cone age were derived from data for all cones on 10 16-year-old plants
121	
122	| Regression model | d.f. | *r* | *F* | *P* |
123	|---|---|---|---|---|
124	| **eqn 1.** New cones per year by plant age: ln (# cones) = 3.61 (ln (plant age)) – 0.14 (plant age) –5.12 | 2,123 | 0.81 | 118.3 | < 0.0001 |
125	| **eqn 2.** Potential seeds per plant: (a) Potential seeds = 12.08(2)(total cones on plant) | | | | |
126	| **eqn 2.** Potential seeds per plant: (b) Potential seeds = 23.75(total cones on plant) –1.11 | 1,122 | 0.89 | 465.6 | < 0.0001 |
127	| **eqn 3.** Open follicles (proportion of total per cone age): ln (proportion follicles open) = 0.48(cone age) –5.27 | 1,94 | 0.85 | 236.6 | < 0.0001 |

132	
133	therefore be described by the simple equation: number of potential seeds = (number of cones)(number of follicles)(2). On average, cones contained 12.08 ± 0.04 follicles, with no significant trend in relation to plant age (Fig. 2a). Although each follicle contained two seeds, only 83.0 ± 1.0% of seeds were firm (i.e. had developed embryos). Viability of firm seeds was variable between years (overall mean 74.4 ± 17.8%), but differences were not significant (Fig. 2b).
134	
135	### SEROTINY, GRANIVORY, DECAY AND SEED STORAGE
136	
137	In the absence of fire nearly all follicles remained closed for the first 5 years. Thereafter the rate of spontaneous seed release increased linearly (Fig. 2c, Table 1). After 10–12 years the cones were heavily weathered and many of the seeds decomposed so that few viable seeds remained.
138	
139	Since plants only began to set viable seed at an age of about 5 years, and little spontaneous follicle rupture occurred in cones less than 5 years old, there was almost no seed loss due to follicle rupture in plants up to 10 years old. Above this age, the percentage seed loss increased markedly: 5% of all follicles on plants were open by age 13 years, 10% by 16 years, and 20% by age 21 years. No seedlings which established in the sample plots as a result of interfire seed release survived for more than one year.
140	
141	The decline in seed storage with cone age was also attributable to seed loss through granivory and decay (Table 1). Loss of seeds through fungal decay followed a similar pattern to that described for spontaneous seed release due to follicle rupture in the absence of fire. Decay was almost absent until cones were 6 years old, after which the proportion of seeds lost increased rapidly.
142	
143	Granivory within closed follicles by the larvae of two weevils, *Cechides amoenus* (Curculionidae; Cleoninae) and *Eleale aulicodes* (Curculionidae; Cleridae), and a jewel beetle (Bupestridae; *Astraeus* sp.) was observed. Unlike follicle opening and decay, granivory was recorded for all cone ages (Table 1).
144	
145	### THE SEED BANK DYNAMICS MODEL
146	
147	By integrating the information on average patterns of seed production, storage and loss in relation to plant and cone age, it was possible to model the pattern of storage of viable seeds on an average plant of any age, and to identify the quantities of seeds lost to incomplete seed development, senescence, interfire dispersal (spontaneous follicle opening), granivory and decay. The statistical relationships used in the model have been described above and are listed in Table 1, and a flow diagram of the model is shown in Fig. 3.
148	
149	The model first estimated the number of new cones produced per year for each plant age up to 25 years using eqn 1 (Table 1). Number of cones per year was set to 17 once plant age reached 15 years (the average for years 15-21). Estimation was stopped at age 25 years since field data were only available for plants up to 21 years. The number of cones was summed for each possible plant age to produce an estimate of the total number of cones held in the crown at any plant age. The total number of seeds which could be held on the plant, if every follicle on every cone held two seeds, was then determined. Two estimation methods were available and gave almost identical results: one based on mean follicle number per cone for samples
150	
151	© 1996 British Ecological Society, *Journal of Ecology*, **84**, 9-17
152	
153	<!-- PAGE BREAK -->
154	
155	13 N. J. Enright *et al.*
156	
157	[Graphs: (a) NO. OF FOLLICLES PER CONE against cone age 0-14; (b) germination (%) 0-100; (c) follicles open (%) 0-100 against CONE AGE (Y) 0-12]
158	
159	**Fig. 2** (a) The number of follicles per cone (± SE) in relation to cone age, (b) percentage germination of firm seeds extracted from closed follicles on cones of different age, and (c) proportion of follicles per cone which opened spontaneously in the absence of fire in relation to cone age for *Banksia hookeriana* near Mt Adams, Western Australia. Note: error bars are not included for data points where sample size was less than 10 cones, or five replicate batches of seeds, per cone age class.
160	
161	of 10 cones per plant (eqn 2a), and another based on complete follicle counts for all cones on a total of 123 plants (eqn 2b). The latter method of estimation was used in the model.
162	
163	The proportion of seeds lost from cones due to spontaneous follicle rupture in the absence of fire was estimated for each cone age (eqn 3) and multiplied by the estimated number of seeds in that age class. A new total for remaining seeds by plant age was then determined. The total number of seeds remaining was multiplied by the proportion of firm seeds (eqn 4) to eliminate aborted seeds held in closed follicles from future calculations. The proportions of firm seeds lost to granivory and decay were estimated for each cone age class (eqns 5 and 6) and deducted from the seeds available within that age class. Finally, the estimated number of viable seeds remaining on a plant of given age was obtained by multiplying the total firm seeds after losses to granivory and decay by the germination rate for firm seeds.
164	
165	Predicted total seeds produced per plant by age 25 years was 5800. Plants were likely, on average, to hold 100 viable seeds in closed follicles by the time they were 8 years old, 1000 by the time they were 17 years, and 1400 when they were 25 years (Fig. 4). The annual rate of viable seed accumulation in the crown peaked at 15 years. By the time plants were 25 years old, the combined impacts of follicle rupture in the absence of fire, and decay, resulted in little further net accumulation of viable seed in the plant canopy and more seeds were lost than were gained per year (Fig. 4). The overall canopy seed store represented a declining proportion of the total seeds produced, dropping from about one-half at age 8 years to one-quarter at age 25 years.
166	
167	Shannon–Weiner diversity (H′) of seed ages represented in the canopy seed bank increased continuously with plant age following the onset of reproductive maturity; quickly at first as the number of seed ages represented increased on young plants (H′ = 0.66 at 6 years, to H′ = 2.00 at 15 years), and then more slowly as the number of seed ages represented on the plant stabilised (H′ = 2.28 at 25 years). The continued increase in H′ after annual seed production had peaked (15 years) and the number of seed ages represented had stabilised (18 years), resulted from increasing evenness (V′) of seed abundance in each age class. Evenness was initially high (V′ = 0.95 at 6 years), declined as each year's seed crop increased (V′ = 0.80 at 17 years), then increased again as seed production stabilised (V′ = 0.88 at 25 years).
168	
169	## Discussion
170	
171	### SEED DEMOGRAPHY
172	
173	Flowering in *Banksia hookeriana* commenced at an age of 3-4 years, but few or no viable seeds were stored on plants <5 years old, so that recurrent fire within this time would lead to loss of the species from the community. The time to first reproduction is similar to that described for a number of other serotinous, nonsprouting trees and shrubs in southern and eastern Australian scrub-heaths (Bradstock 1985;
174

176

The annual production of cones and seeds increased rapidly between ages 5 and 15 years but then fluctuated around a mean of 17 cones per year. This early levelling-off of reproduction is in contrast to the continuous increase in seed production with age noted for *Banksia cuneata* to at least 23 years (Lamont *et al.* 1991b), and for *Banksia ornata* to as much as 38 years (Gill & McMahon 1986).

188	
189	Despite large year to year variations in cone production, on average the total number of cones in the crown showed a steady increase with age. McMaster & Zedler (1981), Lamont *et al.* (1991a), and others hypothesized that canopy seed storage (serotiny) may dampen annual fluctuations in production, ensuring adequate seed supply following fire. The present results support this contention: seeds produced in years of high seed production were nearly all held on the plant for at least 5 years so that years of low seed production did not impact in the short term on the total canopy seed store.
190	
191	Cowling *et al.* (1987) found that years of high seed production were associated with low rates of predispersal granivory by insects, implying satiation of granivores. If serotiny dampens fluctuations in seed availability, as suggested above, then these year to year variations would not prove effective in limiting the impacts of insect granivores unless granivory were

199	restricted to follicles on cones less than one year old. Indeed, Scott (1982) claimed that granivory was concentrated on new cones since the largely host-specific insect larvae which eat *Banksia* seeds can only tunnel through the soft central axis of the inflorescence. He argued that the increasing woodiness of cones with age rendered those more than 1-year-old less vulnerable to invasion. However, Cowling *et al.* (1987) concluded that follicle damage from insects occurred in older cones for *Banksia menziesii* and *Banksia prionotes*. A similar finding was obtained here for *Banksia hookeriana* (Table 1): While granivory was greatest in 1-year-old follicles (18%), it continued at a rate of 2–3% of follicles per year in cones of increasing age. Zammit & Westoby (1988) also recorded granivory in old cones of *Banksia ericifolia* at Ku-ring-gai Chase National Park, New South Wales, but suggested that the trend might be explained by higher rates of infestation in the first few years of seed production when fewer inflorescences were available. However, levels of granivory in cones harvested from young stands provided only limited support for this explanation.
200	
201	### SEED BANK DYNAMICS AND FIRE FREQUENCY
202	
203	According to Gill (1981) plants are not adapted to fire *per se*, but to a particular fire regime. The number of viable seeds stored in the crown of serotinous plants may largely determine the number offspring left after a fire. The balance between the accumulation of viable seeds in the canopy seed bank as plant age increases, and the loss of viable seeds to spontaneous follicle opening, granivory and decay might appropriately describe the optimum life history strategy for a nonsprouting species in relation to fire frequency. The canopy seed bank dynamics model estimates these patterns of accumulation and loss.
204	
205	Early in the reproductive life of individuals of *Banksia hookeriana* (5–8 years of age) few viable seeds are produced, but few are lost. The absolute number of seeds available for dispersal following fire is small and there is a low likelihood of successful parent replacement given the high rates of seed and seedling mortality typical of the first few years following fire (Enright & Lamont 1989, 1992a,b). Using data on seedling recruitment after fire in Little Desert National Park, Victoria, Gill & McMahon (1986) estimated that parent replacement in *Banksia ornata* populations was unlikely until plants held ≈ 100 viable seeds in the crown. This correlated with a plant age of about 16 years. Independent evidence on recruitment of *Banksia hookeriana* near Mt Adams following experimental fires in 1983 and a wildfire in 1984 indicated that between 45 and 90 seeds were released for each recruit still alive in 1990 at the age of 6 or 7 years (Enright & Lamont 1992b). If it is assumed that 100 seeds are required to ensure parent replacement following fire, then the minimum postfire interval for *Banksia hookeriana* plants would be at least 8 years.
206	
207	The total number of viable seeds lost from the canopy during the interfire period increased rapidly with age for plants > 10 years old. Nevertheless, the excess of total viable seeds produced in the plant's lifetime over total losses peaked at age 15 years. As plants continued to age in the absence of fire, total losses approached and finally exceeded the number of viable seeds still in the crown. This was predicted to occur for the average plant by the age of 22 years.
208	
209	Using the simplifying assumption that self-replacement, on average, required release of at least 100 viable seeds per parent after fire, an estimate of the finite rate of natural increase (λ) can be calculated for each plant age (= fire frequency) with the maximum value of λ assumed to reflect the optimum strategy (λ as a measure of fitness, *sensu* Stearns 1992). Populations of *Banksia hookeriana* near Mt Adams appear optimally adapted to recurrent fires every 16–17 years (Fig. 5). Fires at this frequency also maximized the number of viable seeds released after fire relative to the total investment of energy and nutrients expended on seed production. Although the size of the canopy seed bank continued to grow until plants were about 25 years old, predicted λ decreased as plant age increased beyond 17 years. In addition, increasingly more resources are wasted on seeds which perish during the interfire period through spontaneous release into a highly competitive environment where successful recruitment is unlikely, and through predispersal granivory and decay.
210	
211	However, the predicted optimum fire frequency is dependent upon the estimated number of seeds needed to ensure parent replacement. If this estimate is reduced (greater likelihood of recruitment per seed) then the optimum occurs earlier, while if it is increased

It is likely that the true value varies from fire to fire, reflecting differences in the suitability of weather conditions for postfire recruitment (Enright & Lamont 1992a,b). For estimates ranging from half (50) to twice (200) the hypothesized number of seeds required per parent (relative to that used above), the optimum fire frequency ranges from 15 to 18 years, respectively (Fig. 5), and so appears quite robust.
224	
225	If stands remain unburned for more than 25 years, opportunities for interfire recruitment might increase due to the release of sites within stands resulting from death of old individuals. However, Bond (1980) documents the decline of serotinous Proteaceae populations in South African fynbos which have remained unburned for 30-65 years, and we have recorded no successful interfire recruitment to reproductive age in *Banksia hookeriana* for stands up to 21 years old. The lack of older sites precludes further direct study of this question. The wastage of scarce resources (i.e. seed loss) in plants older than 22 years might imply that, historically, sites rarely reach this age before fire recurs. In support of this contention, we have been unable to locate any sites containing plants older than 23 years (Enright & Lamont unpublished data). However, this may also reflect a recent increase in fire frequency due to human interference.
226	
227	Diversity and evenness in the canopy seed store modelled here had not peaked by the estimated optimum return time for fire. Nevertheless, diversity (H′) rises only slowly once this optimum is passed and evenness is always high. One possible consequence of dormant seed banks is the presence of seeds produced in different years which might reflect different pollen parents and selective forces (Harper 1977), i.e. it increases genetic diversity of the seed pool. This might help to buffer the species against rapid evolutionary drift, and at the same time increase resilience of the species in the face of fluctuating environmental conditions. These advantages apply to short-lived species characterized by soil seed storage where parent plants represent different generations. The advantages for longer lived, cohort regenerator species such as *Banksia hookeriana* are less obvious, as all or most pollen will derive from neighbours of identical age which were recruited following the same disturbance and have experienced similar growing conditions. Instead, selfing would probably increase with age as flower head production per plant and death of neighbours increased, cancelling out increasing seed age diversity. Cowling (1987) argued that serotinous nonsprouting species (such as *Banksia hookeriana*) are prone to strong selection pressure, particularly at the seedling stage. He considered that the high number of discrete sexual generations, and fragmentation of populations through fire-mediated local extinction, implies a rapid evolutionary rate and may explain the high level of speciation in *Banksia* and other taxa with similar life histories.
228	
229	The recent history of fire within the geographical range of *Banksia hookeriana* suggests shorter intervals between successive fires than we propose as optimal for species' maintenance. A wildfire in January 1984 burned 117 000 ha of the northern sandplain heath (van der Moezel *et al.* 1987), an area equivalent to nearly half of the total geographical range of the species. In the autumn of 1991 wildfire again covered part of the 1984 burn area near Mt Adams, a return period of only 7 years. This fire eliminated *Banksia hookeriana* from one of the plots enumerated here. Van der Moezel *et al.* (1987) comment that areas of sandplain heath vegetation older than 11 years are becoming increasingly scarce since the establishment of farms and roads in the area and a hazard-reduction burning policy for the remaining natural vegetation.

# Canopy seed bank dynamics and optimum fire regime for the highly serotinous shrub, *Banksia hookeriana*

N.J. ENRIGHT,\*† BYRON B. LAMONT† and RALF MARSULA‡

\*Department of Geography and Environmental Studies, University of Melbourne, Parkville, 3052, Australia, †School of Environmental Biology, Curtin University of Technology, GPO Box U1987 Perth, 6001, Australia and ‡Sektion Ökosystemanalyse, UFZ-Umweltforschungszentrum, Leipzig-Halle GmbH, Permoserstr. 15, PF 2, O-7050 Leipzig, Germany

## Summary

1 *Banksia hookeriana* is a serotinous nonsprouting shrub restricted to the fire-prone northern sandplain scrub-heaths of Western Australia. Evidence of the natural fire frequency to which the species is best adapted was sought through analysis of its seed demography using a computer model of canopy seed bank dynamics based on field data.

2 Plants began flowering at 3-4 years of age but storage of viable seeds in the canopy was rare for plants < 5 years. Infructescences (cones) contained a mean of 12 follicles, holding two seeds of which 62% were estimated to be viable.

3 Cone (and seed) production increased with plant age to 15 years, but then fluctuated widely around a mean of 17 cones per year. By this time the average plant had an estimated canopy seed bank of 700 viable seeds comprising seeds 1–10 years old.

4 Seeds were lost from the canopy seed bank through spontaneous follicle rupture (i.e. in the absence of fire), granivory by insect larvae, and decay. Most follicles remained closed for at least 5 years and up to 50% of follicles were still closed after 10 years. Insect granivores destroyed 18% of seeds in 1-year-old cones, and continued to destroy seeds in older cones at a rate of 2-3% per year.

5 The seed bank model predicted continued seed accumulation in the canopy to at least age 25 years (1400 seeds), but by this time more viable seeds (~ 2200) had been lost to spontaneous opening, granivory and decay than were then stored on the plant.

6 Shannon–Weiner diversity (H′) of seed ages in the canopy seed bank increased with plant age, while evenness (V′) decreased at first (to plant age 17 years) and then increased.

7 On a time-scale of many generations, the likelihood of successful recruitment of individuals in the next generation (on average), occurs for a fire frequency of 15-18 years. At this frequency resource wastage in this low-nutrient environment would be minimized.

8 Recent fires have recurred within 7-11 years and indicate a human impact on the natural fire regime which may ultimately threaten the species.

*Keywords*: *Banksia*, fire frequency, seed bank model, seed demography, serotiny

*Journal of Ecology* (1996) **84**, 9-17

## Introduction

Serotiny refers to the retention of seeds in closed fruits within the plant canopy for more than one year, and can be contrasted with two alternative fates of seeds: storage in a soil seed bank, or release of short-lived seeds upon maturity (no seed storage) (Lamont *et al.* 1991a). Seed release in serotinous species is normally triggered by fire and seeds are short-lived after release, germinating during the first favourable period (Cowling & Lamont 1987). Species can range from weakly serotinous, where most seeds are released within a few years of production, to strongly serotinous, where seeds are held in the canopy for many years. The

© 1996 British Ecological Society

<!-- PAGE BREAK -->

10 Canopy seed bank dynamics in *Banksia hookeriana*

ecological significance of serotiny seems clear: where conditions for seedling recruitment are best immediately following fire (i.e. competition for light, moisture and nutrients are probably at their minimum), cued release of canopy-stored seeds after fire maximizes the age, and therefore canopy seed store, of the population by the time of the next fire. Any seedlings that establish later during the interfire period have a low probability of survival due to competition with their parents and other established plants (Cowling & Lamont 1987; Lamont & Barker 1988). They will be much younger and, on average, will have a smaller canopy seed bank when fire recurs and so are less fit (*sensu* Stearns 1992).

The dynamics of seed production, storage and loss in relation to plant age determines the range of fire frequencies for which population maintenance is possible. If fire occurs either before the onset of reproductive maturity, or before a sufficient canopy seed bank has accumulated, then a population is threatened with extinction.

In the absence of fire some seeds are released by the spontaneous opening of old fruits, but the likelihood of plant recruitment and survival to reproductive age is extremely low. Seed release is hastened by the death of stem tissue due to drought stress and plant senescence (Witkowski *et al.* 1991). This means that the canopy seed bank may be completely lost where plant death occurs before the next fire, a fate not shared by most soil seed bank species where seeds may survive for many years after the death of parent plants (Baker 1989). Because dry plant biomass is more readily consumed by fire, any seeds held in the canopy of dead plants at the time of fire are also likely to perish (Lamont & Barker 1988).

*Banksia hookeriana* Meissn. (Proteaceae) is a highly serotinous, fire-killed (nonsprouting) woody shrub to 2.5 m high which is restricted to the northern sandplain scrub-heaths of south-western Australia about 250-330 km north of Perth (George 1981; Taylor & Hopper 1988). Seeds are held in a state of enforced dormancy within woody follicles on large infructescences (cones) in the crown. While new inflorescences may be damaged and removed from plants by birds, mature cones normally remain attached to the plant throughout its life. Some seeds abort during development, while others are either released gradually or (especially after fire) are consumed by insects, lose viability and decay, or remain viable. Once released seeds germinate with the onset of winter rains or perish as there is no persistent soil seed bank (Enright & Lamont 1989).

The geographical extent (80 × 30 km) of the low nutrient, noncalcareous, sandplain defines the distribution of this species, which is further limited by its specific preference for the deeper sands of low dune crests (Enright & Lamont 1989; Lamont *et al.* 1989). This means that the species exists as a large number of discrete populations of varying sizes (< 100 to > 10 000 individuals) separated by distances of 0.2 to > 1 km. The largest populations are located near Mt Adams in the northern part of the species range. Land clearance for agriculture, mining and mineral exploration, and increased incidence of anthropogenic ignition, make habitat loss and increased fire frequency potential threats to the long term survival of this species. In addition, its attractive orange inflorescences are harvested in large numbers for the commercial wildflower trade, so reducing seed production in exploited populations (Witkowski *et al.* 1994).

This paper describes seed production and availability, and a computer model of seed bank dynamics in *Banksia hookeriana* in relation to plant age (= time since last fire) for sites near Mt Adams. The following questions were posed:

1 What is the pattern of seed production with plant age, and what factors influence the rate of seed accumulation in the crown (e.g. level of serotiny, granivory, seed abortion and longevity)?

2 Does the analysis of seed demography reveal the optimum fire frequency to which the species is adapted, and the range of fire frequencies compatible with population survival?

### STUDY AREA

The study was located in the Yardanogo Nature Reserve about 330 km north of Perth (29°25′S, 114°58′E). Mean annual rainfall at the two closest climate stations is 513 mm (Eneabba; 55 km to the south) and 471 mm (Dongara; 25 km to the north), respectively. There is a pronounced winter maximum with almost no rain (median 20 mm) in the five summer months from December to April. Temperature regimes are similar for both climate stations: mean maximum temperature in the hottest month (January) is 35.8 °C, mean minimum temperature in the coolest month (July) is 9.2 °C. Soils vary from acidic, leached sands on low dunes to sandy clays in intervening depressions (Hnatiuk & Hopkins 1981). The vegetation of the low dunes is a diverse scrub-heath usually dominated by two *Banksia* species, *Banksia hookeriana* and *Banksia attenuata* R. Br., although up to six banksias may co-occur (Beard 1984; Enright & Lamont 1989).

## Materials and methods

Seven sample plots, each 400 m² in area and ranging in age since last fire from 1 to 3 and 14-16 years, were established in 1986 and monitored for 6-8 years. They were on the crests and slopes of low, sandy dunes in scrub-heath along the edge of a 2-km section of Mt Adams Road within the Yardanogo Nature Reserve. Sites covering a broader range of *Banksia hookeriana* stand ages could not be located.

© 1996 British Ecological Society, *Journal of Ecology*, **84**, 9-17

<!-- PAGE BREAK -->

11 N.J. Enright *et al.*

For the five plots where plant age was 1-3 years at the start of the study, and when fire occurred subsequently during the study period (wildfire killed all plants in four of these five plots in 1991), age at time of last fire was estimated for 10 plants by the stem node ageing method described by Lamont (1985), or was known precisely. Seed production was estimated by counting the total number of cones on a random sample of 10 plants and the number of follicles on each of 10 randomly chosen cones per plant. The onset and level of flower head (inflorescence) and cone (infructescence) production were recorded within five replicate 25-m² subplots per plot for each year until 1991 (four plots) or 1993 (one plot).

For the two plots where plant age was 14-16 years in 1986, the total number of plants and total number of cones per plant was determined. For a random sample of 10 plants per plot, the height and crown diameter, and number of new cones was enumerated each year there-after until 1991 (when wildfire killed all plants in one plot) or 1993. Plots were searched each year for evidence of seedling establishment from spontaneous release of seeds in the absence of fire.

Complete cone crops were harvested from 10 randomly chosen 16-year-old plants at the start of the study in 1986. Cones were allocated to annual age classes using the stem node ageing method so that the entire history of reproduction could be determined for each plant. Degree of serotiny was based on the proportion of follicles per cone age class which had opened in the absence of fire (Cowling & Lamont 1985a). Cones were burned and subjected to wet-dry cycles to induce follicle rupture and facilitate seed removal (Cowling & Lamont 1985b). The numbers of follicles, and proportions of firm, aborted, eaten and decayed seeds were determined per plant by cone age. Viability of firm seeds was assessed by germinating batches of 25 seeds per cone age class from each of five plants (replicates) under moist conditions at 15 °C (Cowling *et al.* 1987).

### STATISTICAL ANALYSES

Trends between seed parameters, plant age and cone age were analysed using regression models (SYSTAT 1992). Where data were not normally distributed, logarithmic (ln) and arcsine transformations were employed to satisfy assumptions of the regression models used. All error terms listed are standard errors.

A canopy seed bank dynamics model, written in programming language C++, was used to estimate the pattern of viable seed retention on plants and fate of seeds in relation to age. The model used regression equations and other statistics relating patterns of seed accumulation and loss to increasing plant and cone age. Shannon–Weiner diversity (H′) and evenness (V′) were calculated for the distribution of viable seed ages by plant age.

## Results

### CONE PRODUCTION

A few plants produced inflorescences at 3-4 years of age, but these were all sterile (age 3: mean inflorescences per plant = 0.12 ± 0.06; age 4: mean = 0.92 ± 0.23). Plants first produced fertile cones at an age of 5 years. Cone production increased until plants were about 15 years old, after which annual production fluctuated widely about an average of 17 cones per year (Fig. 1a; Table 1). Both within and between year variability in cone production per plant increased with plant age.

The total number of cones held in the crown increased continuously with plant age and although the standard error also increased with age, the mean pattern of accumulation showed a consistent trend (Fig. 1b, Table 1).

### SEROTINY, GRANIVORY, DECAY AND SEED STORAGE

In the absence of fire nearly all follicles remained closed for the first 5 years. Thereafter the rate of spontaneous seed release increased linearly (Fig. 2c, Table 1). After 10–12 years the cones were heavily weathered and many of the seeds decomposed so that few viable seeds remained.

Since plants only began to set viable seed at an age of about 5 years, and little spontaneous follicle rupture occurred in cones less than 5 years old, there was almost no seed loss due to follicle rupture in plants up to 10 years old. Above this age, the percentage seed loss increased markedly: 5% of all follicles on plants were open by age 13 years, 10% by 16 years, and 20% by age 21 years. No seedlings which established in the sample plots as a result of interfire seed release survived for more than one year.

The decline in seed storage with cone age was also attributable to seed loss through granivory and decay (Table 1). Loss of seeds through fungal decay followed a similar pattern to that described for spontaneous seed release due to follicle rupture in the absence of fire. Decay was almost absent until cones were 6 years old, after which the proportion of seeds lost increased rapidly.

Granivory within closed follicles by the larvae of two weevils, *Cechides amoenus* (Curculionidae; Cleoninae) and *Eleale aulicodes* (Curculionidae; Cleridae), and a jewel beetle (Bupestridae; *Astraeus* sp.) was observed. Unlike follicle opening and decay, granivory was recorded for all cone ages (Table 1).

### THE SEED BANK DYNAMICS MODEL

By integrating the information on average patterns of seed production, storage and loss in relation to plant and cone age, it was possible to model the pattern of storage of viable seeds on an average plant of any age, and to identify the quantities of seeds lost to incomplete seed development, senescence, interfire dispersal (spontaneous follicle opening), granivory and decay. The statistical relationships used in the model have been described above and are listed in Table 1, and a flow diagram of the model is shown in Fig. 3.

The model first estimated the number of new cones produced per year for each plant age up to 25 years using eqn 1 (Table 1). Number of cones per year was set to 17 once plant age reached 15 years (the average for years 15-21). Estimation was stopped at age 25 years since field data were only available for plants up to 21 years. The number of cones was summed for each possible plant age to produce an estimate of the total number of cones held in the crown at any plant age. The total number of seeds which could be held on the plant, if every follicle on every cone held two seeds, was then determined. Two estimation methods were available and gave almost identical results: one based on mean follicle number per cone for samples
