Predicted total seeds produced per plant by age 25 years was 5800. Plants were likely, on average, to hold 100 viable seeds in closed follicles by the time they were 8 years old, 1000 by the time they were 17 years, and 1400 when they were 25 years (Fig. 4). The annual rate of viable seed accumulation in the crown peaked at 15 years. By the time plants were 25 years old, the combined impacts of follicle rupture in the absence of fire, and decay, resulted in little further net accumulation of viable seed in the plant canopy and more seeds were lost than were gained per year (Fig. 4). The overall canopy seed store represented a declining proportion of the total seeds produced, dropping from about one-half at age 8 years to one-quarter at age 25 years.

Shannon–Weiner diversity (H′) of seed ages represented in the canopy seed bank increased continuously with plant age following the onset of reproductive maturity; quickly at first as the number of seed ages represented increased on young plants (H′ = 0.66 at 6 years, to H′ = 2.00 at 15 years), and then more slowly as the number of seed ages represented on the plant stabilised (H′ = 2.28 at 25 years). The continued increase in H′ after annual seed production had peaked (15 years) and the number of seed ages represented had stabilised (18 years), resulted from increasing evenness (V′) of seed abundance in each age class. Evenness was initially high (V′ = 0.95 at 6 years), declined as each year's seed crop increased (V′ = 0.80 at 17 years), then increased again as seed production stabilised (V′ = 0.88 at 25 years).

## Discussion

### SEED DEMOGRAPHY

Flowering in *Banksia hookeriana* commenced at an age of 3-4 years, but few or no viable seeds were stored on plants <5 years old, so that recurrent fire within this time would lead to loss of the species from the community. The time to first reproduction is similar to that described for a number of other serotinous, nonsprouting trees and shrubs in southern and eastern Australian scrub-heaths (Bradstock 1985;

The annual production of cones and seeds increased rapidly between ages 5 and 15 years but then fluctuated around a mean of 17 cones per year. This early levelling-off of reproduction is in contrast to the continuous increase in seed production with age noted for *Banksia cuneata* to at least 23 years (Lamont *et al.* 1991b), and for *Banksia ornata* to as much as 38 years (Gill & McMahon 1986).

Despite large year to year variations in cone production, on average the total number of cones in the crown showed a steady increase with age. McMaster & Zedler (1981), Lamont *et al.* (1991a), and others hypothesized that canopy seed storage (serotiny) may dampen annual fluctuations in production, ensuring adequate seed supply following fire. The present results support this contention: seeds produced in years of high seed production were nearly all held on the plant for at least 5 years so that years of low seed production did not impact in the short term on the total canopy seed store.

Cowling *et al.* (1987) found that years of high seed production were associated with low rates of predispersal granivory by insects, implying satiation of granivores. If serotiny dampens fluctuations in seed availability, as suggested above, then these year to year variations would not prove effective in limiting the impacts of insect granivores unless granivory were

restricted to follicles on cones less than one year old. Indeed, Scott (1982) claimed that granivory was concentrated on new cones since the largely host-specific insect larvae which eat *Banksia* seeds can only tunnel through the soft central axis of the inflorescence. He argued that the increasing woodiness of cones with age rendered those more than 1-year-old less vulnerable to invasion. However, Cowling *et al.* (1987) concluded that follicle damage from insects occurred in older cones for *Banksia menziesii* and *Banksia prionotes*. A similar finding was obtained here for *Banksia hookeriana* (Table 1): While granivory was greatest in 1-year-old follicles (18%), it continued at a rate of 2–3% of follicles per year in cones of increasing age. Zammit & Westoby (1988) also recorded granivory in old cones of *Banksia ericifolia* at Ku-ring-gai Chase National Park, New South Wales, but suggested that the trend might be explained by higher rates of infestation in the first few years of seed production when fewer inflorescences were available. However, levels of granivory in cones harvested from young stands provided only limited support for this explanation.

### SEED BANK DYNAMICS AND FIRE FREQUENCY

According to Gill (1981) plants are not adapted to fire *per se*, but to a particular fire regime. The number of viable seeds stored in the crown of serotinous plants may largely determine the number offspring left after a fire. The balance between the accumulation of viable seeds in the canopy seed bank as plant age increases, and the loss of viable seeds to spontaneous follicle opening, granivory and decay might appropriately describe the optimum life history strategy for a nonsprouting species in relation to fire frequency. The canopy seed bank dynamics model estimates these patterns of accumulation and loss.

Early in the reproductive life of individuals of *Banksia hookeriana* (5–8 years of age) few viable seeds are produced, but few are lost. The absolute number of seeds available for dispersal following fire is small and there is a low likelihood of successful parent replacement given the high rates of seed and seedling mortality typical of the first few years following fire (Enright & Lamont 1989, 1992a,b). Using data on seedling recruitment after fire in Little Desert National Park, Victoria, Gill & McMahon (1986) estimated that parent replacement in *Banksia ornata* populations was unlikely until plants held ≈ 100 viable seeds in the crown. This correlated with a plant age of about 16 years. Independent evidence on recruitment of *Banksia hookeriana* near Mt Adams following experimental fires in 1983 and a wildfire in 1984 indicated that between 45 and 90 seeds were released for each recruit still alive in 1990 at the age of 6 or 7 years (Enright & Lamont 1992b). If it is assumed that 100 seeds are required to ensure parent replacement following fire, then the minimum postfire interval for *Banksia hookeriana* plants would be at least 8 years.

The total number of viable seeds lost from the canopy during the interfire period increased rapidly with age for plants > 10 years old. Nevertheless, the excess of total viable seeds produced in the plant's lifetime over total losses peaked at age 15 years. As plants continued to age in the absence of fire, total losses approached and finally exceeded the number of viable seeds still in the crown. This was predicted to occur for the average plant by the age of 22 years.

Using the simplifying assumption that self-replacement, on average, required release of at least 100 viable seeds per parent after fire, an estimate of the finite rate of natural increase (λ) can be calculated for each plant age (= fire frequency) with the maximum value of λ assumed to reflect the optimum strategy (λ as a measure of fitness, *sensu* Stearns 1992). Populations of *Banksia hookeriana* near Mt Adams appear optimally adapted to recurrent fires every 16–17 years (Fig. 5). Fires at this frequency also maximized the number of viable seeds released after fire relative to the total investment of energy and nutrients expended on seed production. Although the size of the canopy seed bank continued to grow until plants were about 25 years old, predicted λ decreased as plant age increased beyond 17 years. In addition, increasingly more resources are wasted on seeds which perish during the interfire period through spontaneous release into a highly competitive environment where successful recruitment is unlikely, and through predispersal granivory and decay.

However, the predicted optimum fire frequency is dependent upon the estimated number of seeds needed to ensure parent replacement. If this estimate is reduced (greater likelihood of recruitment per seed) then the optimum occurs earlier, while if it is increased

(less likelihood of recruitment) the optimum occurs later. It is likely that the true value varies from fire to fire, reflecting differences in the suitability of weather conditions for postfire recruitment (Enright & Lamont 1992a,b). For estimates ranging from half (50) to twice (200) the hypothesized number of seeds required per parent (relative to that used above), the optimum fire frequency ranges from 15 to 18 years, respectively (Fig. 5), and so appears quite robust.

If stands remain unburned for more than 25 years, opportunities for interfire recruitment might increase due to the release of sites within stands resulting from death of old individuals. However, Bond (1980) documents the decline of serotinous Proteaceae populations in South African fynbos which have remained unburned for 30-65 years, and we have recorded no successful interfire recruitment to reproductive age in *Banksia hookeriana* for stands up to 21 years old. The lack of older sites precludes further direct study of this question. The wastage of scarce resources (i.e. seed loss) in plants older than 22 years might imply that, historically, sites rarely reach this age before fire recurs. In support of this contention, we have been unable to locate any sites containing plants older than 23 years (Enright & Lamont unpublished data). However, this may also reflect a recent increase in fire frequency due to human interference.

Diversity and evenness in the canopy seed store modelled here had not peaked by the estimated optimum return time for fire. Nevertheless, diversity (H′) rises only slowly once this optimum is passed and evenness is always high. One possible consequence of dormant seed banks is the presence of seeds produced in different years which might reflect different pollen parents and selective forces (Harper 1977), i.e. it increases genetic diversity of the seed pool. This might help to buffer the species against rapid evolutionary drift, and at the same time increase resilience of the species in the face of fluctuating environmental conditions. These advantages apply to short-lived species characterized by soil seed storage where parent plants represent different generations. The advantages for longer lived, cohort regenerator species such as *Banksia hookeriana* are less obvious, as all or most pollen will derive from neighbours of identical age which were recruited following the same disturbance and have experienced similar growing conditions. Instead, selfing would probably increase with age as flower head production per plant and death of neighbours increased, cancelling out increasing seed age diversity. Cowling (1987) argued that serotinous nonsprouting species (such as *Banksia hookeriana*) are prone to strong selection pressure, particularly at the seedling stage. He considered that the high number of discrete sexual generations, and fragmentation of populations through fire-mediated local extinction, implies a rapid evolutionary rate and may explain the high level of speciation in *Banksia* and other taxa with similar life histories.

The recent history of fire within the geographical range of *Banksia hookeriana* suggests shorter intervals between successive fires than we propose as optimal for species' maintenance. A wildfire in January 1984 burned 117 000 ha of the northern sandplain heath (van der Moezel *et al.* 1987), an area equivalent to nearly half of the total geographical range of the species. In the autumn of 1991 wildfire again covered part of the 1984 burn area near Mt Adams, a return period of only 7 years. This fire eliminated *Banksia hookeriana* from one of the plots enumerated here. Van der Moezel *et al.* (1987) comment that areas of sandplain heath vegetation older than 11 years are becoming increasingly scarce since the establishment of farms and roads in the area and a hazard-reduction burning policy for the remaining natural vegetation.

In all cases, a greater proportion of seedlings occurred further from the adult than suggested by the seed distributions. When the distribution of seeds was compared with that of seedlings around isolated individuals of *D*. *excelsa* at Site 1, there was a difference in the shape of the respective distributions, with the distribution of seedlings fairly uniform up to about 7 m from an adult (Fig. 4). In contrast to the distribution of seeds (Fig. 1*a*), there was not a large proportion of seedlings near adults. These data suggest that seedlings had a similar likelihood of occurring anywhere up to 7 m from their parent. Where there were overlapping seed shadows from parent plants in *D*. *excelsa*, the distribution of seedlings (Fig. 5*a*) was uneven, but more or less uniform in density up to 4 m from a parent plant, with a decline further away. For *T*. *speciosissima*, the overall shape of the distributions of seeds and seedlings was similar, despite the significant difference in the distributions. The greatest proportion of seedlings occurred further from the adult than for seeds and the tail extended further from the adult (Figs 1*b*, 5*b*). The maximum difference in distributions tended to occur within 2 m from adults, suggesting that there is some interaction between adults and seedling recruitment that leads to reduced recruitment less than 2 m from adults. This effect appeared to be most pronounced in *T*. *speciosissima* at Site 1. In both species, recruits were located well beyond the limit of seeds detected in the seed-distribution surveys, suggesting either occasional long-distance dispersal directly from the infructescence or later (i.e. after our survey) dispersal occurring at ground level (Harper 1977; Hammill *et al.* 1998). 220 221 #### **Discussion** 222 223 Both pyrogenic flowering, resprouting species took some 19 months to flower after the January 1994 fire. 18	# Canopy seed bank dynamics and optimum fire regime for the highly serotinous shrub, *Banksia hookeriana*
19	
20	N.J. ENRIGHT,\*† BYRON B. LAMONT† and RALF MARSULA‡
21	
22	\*Department of Geography and Environmental Studies, University of Melbourne, Parkville, 3052, Australia, †School of Environmental Biology, Curtin University of Technology, GPO Box U1987 Perth, 6001, Australia and ‡Sektion Ökosystemanalyse, UFZ-Umweltforschungszentrum, Leipzig-Halle GmbH, Permoserstr. 15, PF 2, O-7050 Leipzig, Germany
23	
24	## Summary
25	
26	1 *Banksia hookeriana* is a serotinous nonsprouting shrub restricted to the fire-prone northern sandplain scrub-heaths of Western Australia. Evidence of the natural fire frequency to which the species is best adapted was sought through analysis of its seed demography using a computer model of canopy seed bank dynamics based on field data.
27	
28	2 Plants began flowering at 3-4 years of age but storage of viable seeds in the canopy was rare for plants < 5 years. Infructescences (cones) contained a mean of 12 follicles, holding two seeds of which 62% were estimated to be viable.
29	
30	3 Cone (and seed) production increased with plant age to 15 years, but then fluctuated widely around a mean of 17 cones per year. By this time the average plant had an estimated canopy seed bank of 700 viable seeds comprising seeds 1–10 years old.
31	
32	4 Seeds were lost from the canopy seed bank through spontaneous follicle rupture (i.e. in the absence of fire), granivory by insect larvae, and decay. Most follicles remained closed for at least 5 years and up to 50% of follicles were still closed after 10 years. Insect granivores destroyed 18% of seeds in 1-year-old cones, and continued to destroy seeds in older cones at a rate of 2-3% per year.
33	
34	5 The seed bank model predicted continued seed accumulation in the canopy to at least age 25 years (1400 seeds), but by this time more viable seeds (~ 2200) had been lost to spontaneous opening, granivory and decay than were then stored on the plant.
35	
36	6 Shannon–Weiner diversity (H′) of seed ages in the canopy seed bank increased with plant age, while evenness (V′) decreased at first (to plant age 17 years) and then increased.
37	
38	7 On a time-scale of many generations, the likelihood of successful recruitment of individuals in the next generation (on average), occurs for a fire frequency of 15-18 years. At this frequency resource wastage in this low-nutrient environment would be minimized.
39	
40	8 Recent fires have recurred within 7-11 years and indicate a human impact on the natural fire regime which may ultimately threaten the species.
41	
42	*Keywords*: *Banksia*, fire frequency, seed bank model, seed demography, serotiny

46	## Introduction
47	
48	Serotiny refers to the retention of seeds in closed fruits within the plant canopy for more than one year, and can be contrasted with two alternative fates of seeds: storage in a soil seed bank, or release of short-lived seeds upon maturity (no seed storage) (Lamont *et al.* 1991a). Seed release in serotinous species is normally triggered by fire and seeds are short-lived after release, germinating during the first favourable period (Cowling & Lamont 1987). Species can range from weakly serotinous, where most seeds are released within a few years of production, to strongly serotinous, where seeds are held in the canopy for many years. The
49	
50	Correspondence: Dr Neal Enright, Department of Geography and Environmental Studies, University of Melbourne, Parkville, 3052, Australia, Fax: 61 393444972, E-mail: Enright@ariel.ucs.unimelb.edu.au

56	10 Canopy seed bank dynamics in *Banksia hookeriana*
57	
58	ecological significance of serotiny seems clear: where conditions for seedling recruitment are best immediately following fire (i.e. competition for light, moisture and nutrients are probably at their minimum), cued release of canopy-stored seeds after fire maximizes the age, and therefore canopy seed store, of the population by the time of the next fire. Any seedlings that establish later during the interfire period have a low probability of survival due to competition with their parents and other established plants (Cowling & Lamont 1987; Lamont & Barker 1988). They will be much younger and, on average, will have a smaller canopy seed bank when fire recurs and so are less fit (*sensu* Stearns 1992).
59	
60	The dynamics of seed production, storage and loss in relation to plant age determines the range of fire frequencies for which population maintenance is possible. If fire occurs either before the onset of reproductive maturity, or before a sufficient canopy seed bank has accumulated, then a population is threatened with extinction.
61	
62	In the absence of fire some seeds are released by the spontaneous opening of old fruits, but the likelihood of plant recruitment and survival to reproductive age is extremely low. Seed release is hastened by the death of stem tissue due to drought stress and plant senescence (Witkowski *et al.* 1991). This means that the canopy seed bank may be completely lost where plant death occurs before the next fire, a fate not shared by most soil seed bank species where seeds may survive for many years after the death of parent plants (Baker 1989). Because dry plant biomass is more readily consumed by fire, any seeds held in the canopy of dead plants at the time of fire are also likely to perish (Lamont & Barker 1988).
63	
64	*Banksia hookeriana* Meissn. (Proteaceae) is a highly serotinous, fire-killed (nonsprouting) woody shrub to 2.5 m high which is restricted to the northern sandplain scrub-heaths of south-western Australia about 250-330 km north of Perth (George 1981; Taylor & Hopper 1988). Seeds are held in a state of enforced dormancy within woody follicles on large infructescences (cones) in the crown. While new inflorescences may be damaged and removed from plants by birds, mature cones normally remain attached to the plant throughout its life. Some seeds abort during development, while others are either released gradually or (especially after fire) are consumed by insects, lose viability and decay, or remain viable. Once released seeds germinate with the onset of winter rains or perish as there is no persistent soil seed bank (Enright & Lamont 1989).
65	
66	The geographical extent (80 × 30 km) of the low nutrient, noncalcareous, sandplain defines the distribution of this species, which is further limited by its specific preference for the deeper sands of low dune crests (Enright & Lamont 1989; Lamont *et al.* 1989). This means that the species exists as a large number of discrete populations of varying sizes (< 100 to > 10 000 individuals) separated by distances of 0.2 to > 1 km. The largest populations are located near Mt Adams in the northern part of the species range. Land clearance for agriculture, mining and mineral exploration, and increased incidence of anthropogenic ignition, make habitat loss and increased fire frequency potential threats to the long term survival of this species. In addition, its attractive orange inflorescences are harvested in large numbers for the commercial wildflower trade, so reducing seed production in exploited populations (Witkowski *et al.* 1994).
67	
68	This paper describes seed production and availability, and a computer model of seed bank dynamics in *Banksia hookeriana* in relation to plant age (= time since last fire) for sites near Mt Adams. The following questions were posed:
69	
70	1 What is the pattern of seed production with plant age, and what factors influence the rate of seed accumulation in the crown (e.g. level of serotiny, granivory, seed abortion and longevity)?
71	
72	2 Does the analysis of seed demography reveal the optimum fire frequency to which the species is adapted, and the range of fire frequencies compatible with population survival?
73	
74	### STUDY AREA
75	
76	The study was located in the Yardanogo Nature Reserve about 330 km north of Perth (29°25′S, 114°58′E). Mean annual rainfall at the two closest climate stations is 513 mm (Eneabba; 55 km to the south) and 471 mm (Dongara; 25 km to the north), respectively. There is a pronounced winter maximum with almost no rain (median 20 mm) in the five summer months from December to April. Temperature regimes are similar for both climate stations: mean maximum temperature in the hottest month (January) is 35.8 °C, mean minimum temperature in the coolest month (July) is 9.2 °C. Soils vary from acidic, leached sands on low dunes to sandy clays in intervening depressions (Hnatiuk & Hopkins 1981). The vegetation of the low dunes is a diverse scrub-heath usually dominated by two *Banksia* species, *Banksia hookeriana* and *Banksia attenuata* R. Br., although up to six banksias may co-occur (Beard 1984; Enright & Lamont 1989).
77	
78	## Materials and methods
79	
80	Seven sample plots, each 400 m² in area and ranging in age since last fire from 1 to 3 and 14-16 years, were established in 1986 and monitored for 6-8 years. They were on the crests and slopes of low, sandy dunes in scrub-heath along the edge of a 2-km section of Mt Adams Road within the Yardanogo Nature Reserve. Sites covering a broader range of *Banksia hookeriana* stand ages could not be located.

88	For the five plots where plant age was 1-3 years at the start of the study, and when fire occurred subsequently during the study period (wildfire killed all plants in four of these five plots in 1991), age at time of last fire was estimated for 10 plants by the stem node ageing method described by Lamont (1985), or was known precisely. Seed production was estimated by counting the total number of cones on a random sample of 10 plants and the number of follicles on each of 10 randomly chosen cones per plant. The onset and level of flower head (inflorescence) and cone (infructescence) production were recorded within five replicate 25-m² subplots per plot for each year until 1991 (four plots) or 1993 (one plot).
89	
90	For the two plots where plant age was 14-16 years in 1986, the total number of plants and total number of cones per plant was determined. For a random sample of 10 plants per plot, the height and crown diameter, and number of new cones was enumerated each year there-after until 1991 (when wildfire killed all plants in one plot) or 1993. Plots were searched each year for evidence of seedling establishment from spontaneous release of seeds in the absence of fire.
91	
92	Complete cone crops were harvested from 10 randomly chosen 16-year-old plants at the start of the study in 1986. Cones were allocated to annual age classes using the stem node ageing method so that the entire history of reproduction could be determined for each plant. Degree of serotiny was based on the proportion of follicles per cone age class which had opened in the absence of fire (Cowling & Lamont 1985a). Cones were burned and subjected to wet-dry cycles to induce follicle rupture and facilitate seed removal (Cowling & Lamont 1985b). The numbers of follicles, and proportions of firm, aborted, eaten and decayed seeds were determined per plant by cone age. Viability of firm seeds was assessed by germinating batches of 25 seeds per cone age class from each of five plants (replicates) under moist conditions at 15 °C (Cowling *et al.* 1987).
93	
94	### STATISTICAL ANALYSES
95	
96	Trends between seed parameters, plant age and cone age were analysed using regression models (SYSTAT 1992). Where data were not normally distributed, logarithmic (ln) and arcsine transformations were employed to satisfy assumptions of the regression models used. All error terms listed are standard errors.
97	
98	A canopy seed bank dynamics model, written in programming language C++, was used to estimate the pattern of viable seed retention on plants and fate of seeds in relation to age. The model used regression equations and other statistics relating patterns of seed accumulation and loss to increasing plant and cone age. Shannon–Weiner diversity (H′) and evenness (V′) were calculated for the distribution of viable seed ages by plant age.
99	
100	## Results
101	
102	### CONE PRODUCTION
103	
104	A few plants produced inflorescences at 3-4 years of age, but these were all sterile (age 3: mean inflorescences per plant = 0.12 ± 0.06; age 4: mean = 0.92 ± 0.23). Plants first produced fertile cones at an age of 5 years. Cone production increased until plants were about 15 years old, after which annual production fluctuated widely about an average of 17 cones per year (Fig. 1a; Table 1). Both within and between year variability in cone production per plant increased with plant age.
105	
106	The total number of cones held in the crown increased continuously with plant age and although the standard error also increased with age, the mean pattern of accumulation showed a consistent trend (Fig. 1b, Table 1).

108	### SEED PRODUCTION
109	
110	Cones of *Banksia hookeriana* contained up to 20 woody follicles, each of which held two seeds. The maximum possible number of seeds on a plant can

135	### SEROTINY, GRANIVORY, DECAY AND SEED STORAGE
136	
137	In the absence of fire nearly all follicles remained closed for the first 5 years. Thereafter the rate of spontaneous seed release increased linearly (Fig. 2c, Table 1). After 10–12 years the cones were heavily weathered and many of the seeds decomposed so that few viable seeds remained.
138	
139	Since plants only began to set viable seed at an age of about 5 years, and little spontaneous follicle rupture occurred in cones less than 5 years old, there was almost no seed loss due to follicle rupture in plants up to 10 years old. Above this age, the percentage seed loss increased markedly: 5% of all follicles on plants were open by age 13 years, 10% by 16 years, and 20% by age 21 years. No seedlings which established in the sample plots as a result of interfire seed release survived for more than one year.
140	
141	The decline in seed storage with cone age was also attributable to seed loss through granivory and decay (Table 1). Loss of seeds through fungal decay followed a similar pattern to that described for spontaneous seed release due to follicle rupture in the absence of fire. Decay was almost absent until cones were 6 years old, after which the proportion of seeds lost increased rapidly.
142	
143	Granivory within closed follicles by the larvae of two weevils, *Cechides amoenus* (Curculionidae; Cleoninae) and *Eleale aulicodes* (Curculionidae; Cleridae), and a jewel beetle (Bupestridae; *Astraeus* sp.) was observed. Unlike follicle opening and decay, granivory was recorded for all cone ages (Table 1).

145	### THE SEED BANK DYNAMICS MODEL
146	
147	By integrating the information on average patterns of seed production, storage and loss in relation to plant and cone age, it was possible to model the pattern of storage of viable seeds on an average plant of any age, and to identify the quantities of seeds lost to incomplete seed development, senescence, interfire dispersal (spontaneous follicle opening), granivory and decay. The statistical relationships used in the model have been described above and are listed in Table 1, and a flow diagram of the model is shown in Fig. 3.

Number of cones per year was set to 17 once plant age reached 15 years (the average for years 15-21). Estimation was stopped at age 25 years since field data were only available for plants up to 21 years. The number of cones was summed for each possible plant age to produce an estimate of the total number of cones held in the crown at any plant age. The total number of seeds which could be held on the plant, if every follicle on every cone held two seeds, was then determined. Two estimation methods were available and gave almost identical results: one based on mean follicle number per cone for samples

165	Predicted total seeds produced per plant by age 25 years was 5800. Plants were likely, on average, to hold 100 viable seeds in closed follicles by the time they were 8 years old, 1000 by the time they were 17 years, and 1400 when they were 25 years (Fig. 4). The annual rate of viable seed accumulation in the crown peaked at 15 years. By the time plants were 25 years old, the combined impacts of follicle rupture in the absence of fire, and decay, resulted in little further net accumulation of viable seed in the plant canopy and more seeds were lost than were gained per year (Fig. 4). The overall canopy seed store represented a declining proportion of the total seeds produced, dropping from about one-half at age 8 years to one-quarter at age 25 years.

The continued increase in H′ after annual seed production had peaked (15 years) and the number of seed ages represented had stabilised (18 years), resulted from increasing evenness (V′) of seed abundance in each age class. Evenness was initially high (V′ = 0.95 at 6 years), declined as each year's seed crop increased (V′ = 0.80 at 17 years), then increased again as seed production stabilised (V′ = 0.88 at 25 years).

169	## Discussion
170	
171	### SEED DEMOGRAPHY
172	
173	Flowering in *Banksia hookeriana* commenced at an age of 3-4 years, but few or no viable seeds were stored on plants <5 years old, so that recurrent fire within this time would lead to loss of the species from the community. The time to first reproduction is similar to that described for a number of other serotinous, nonsprouting trees and shrubs in southern and eastern Australian scrub-heaths (Bradstock 1985;

The annual production of cones and seeds increased rapidly between ages 5 and 15 years but then fluctuated around a mean of 17 cones per year. This early levelling-off of reproduction is in contrast to the continuous increase in seed production with age noted for *Banksia cuneata* to at least 23 years (Lamont *et al.* 1991b), and for *Banksia ornata* to as much as 38 years (Gill & McMahon 1986).

188	
189	Despite large year to year variations in cone production, on average the total number of cones in the crown showed a steady increase with age. McMaster & Zedler (1981), Lamont *et al.* (1991a), and others hypothesized that canopy seed storage (serotiny) may dampen annual fluctuations in production, ensuring adequate seed supply following fire. The present results support this contention: seeds produced in years of high seed production were nearly all held on the plant for at least 5 years so that years of low seed production did not impact in the short term on the total canopy seed store.
190	
191	Cowling *et al.* (1987) found that years of high seed production were associated with low rates of predispersal granivory by insects, implying satiation of granivores. If serotiny dampens fluctuations in seed availability, as suggested above, then these year to year variations would not prove effective in limiting the impacts of insect granivores unless granivory were

199	restricted to follicles on cones less than one year old. Indeed, Scott (1982) claimed that granivory was concentrated on new cones since the largely host-specific insect larvae which eat *Banksia* seeds can only tunnel through the soft central axis of the inflorescence. He argued that the increasing woodiness of cones with age rendered those more than 1-year-old less vulnerable to invasion. However, Cowling *et al.* (1987) concluded that follicle damage from insects occurred in older cones for *Banksia menziesii* and *Banksia prionotes*. A similar finding was obtained here for *Banksia hookeriana* (Table 1): While granivory was greatest in 1-year-old follicles (18%), it continued at a rate of 2–3% of follicles per year in cones of increasing age. Zammit & Westoby (1988) also recorded granivory in old cones of *Banksia ericifolia* at Ku-ring-gai Chase National Park, New South Wales, but suggested that the trend might be explained by higher rates of infestation in the first few years of seed production when fewer inflorescences were available. However, levels of granivory in cones harvested from young stands provided only limited support for this explanation.
200	
201	### SEED BANK DYNAMICS AND FIRE FREQUENCY
202	
203	According to Gill (1981) plants are not adapted to fire *per se*, but to a particular fire regime. The number of viable seeds stored in the crown of serotinous plants may largely determine the number offspring left after a fire. The balance between the accumulation of viable seeds in the canopy seed bank as plant age increases, and the loss of viable seeds to spontaneous follicle opening, granivory and decay might appropriately describe the optimum life history strategy for a nonsprouting species in relation to fire frequency. The canopy seed bank dynamics model estimates these patterns of accumulation and loss.
204	
205	Early in the reproductive life of individuals of *Banksia hookeriana* (5–8 years of age) few viable seeds are produced, but few are lost. The absolute number of seeds available for dispersal following fire is small and there is a low likelihood of successful parent replacement given the high rates of seed and seedling mortality typical of the first few years following fire (Enright & Lamont 1989, 1992a,b). Using data on seedling recruitment after fire in Little Desert National Park, Victoria, Gill & McMahon (1986) estimated that parent replacement in *Banksia ornata* populations was unlikely until plants held ≈ 100 viable seeds in the crown. This correlated with a plant age of about 16 years. Independent evidence on recruitment of *Banksia hookeriana* near Mt Adams following experimental fires in 1983 and a wildfire in 1984 indicated that between 45 and 90 seeds were released for each recruit still alive in 1990 at the age of 6 or 7 years (Enright & Lamont 1992b). If it is assumed that 100 seeds are required to ensure parent replacement following fire, then the minimum postfire interval for *Banksia hookeriana* plants would be at least 8 years.
206	
207	The total number of viable seeds lost from the canopy during the interfire period increased rapidly with age for plants > 10 years old. Nevertheless, the excess of total viable seeds produced in the plant's lifetime over total losses peaked at age 15 years. As plants continued to age in the absence of fire, total losses approached and finally exceeded the number of viable seeds still in the crown. This was predicted to occur for the average plant by the age of 22 years.
208	
209	Using the simplifying assumption that self-replacement, on average, required release of at least 100 viable seeds per parent after fire, an estimate of the finite rate of natural increase (λ) can be calculated for each plant age (= fire frequency) with the maximum value of λ assumed to reflect the optimum strategy (λ as a measure of fitness, *sensu* Stearns 1992). Populations of *Banksia hookeriana* near Mt Adams appear optimally adapted to recurrent fires every 16–17 years (Fig. 5). Fires at this frequency also maximized the number of viable seeds released after fire relative to the total investment of energy and nutrients expended on seed production. Although the size of the canopy seed bank continued to grow until plants were about 25 years old, predicted λ decreased as plant age increased beyond 17 years. In addition, increasingly more resources are wasted on seeds which perish during the interfire period through spontaneous release into a highly competitive environment where successful recruitment is unlikely, and through predispersal granivory and decay.
210	
211	However, the predicted optimum fire frequency is dependent upon the estimated number of seeds needed to ensure parent replacement. If this estimate is reduced (greater likelihood of recruitment per seed) then the optimum occurs earlier, while if it is increased

223	(less likelihood of recruitment) the optimum occurs later. It is likely that the true value varies from fire to fire, reflecting differences in the suitability of weather conditions for postfire recruitment (Enright & Lamont 1992a,b). For estimates ranging from half (50) to twice (200) the hypothesized number of seeds required per parent (relative to that used above), the optimum fire frequency ranges from 15 to 18 years, respectively (Fig. 5), and so appears quite robust.
224	
225	If stands remain unburned for more than 25 years, opportunities for interfire recruitment might increase due to the release of sites within stands resulting from death of old individuals. However, Bond (1980) documents the decline of serotinous Proteaceae populations in South African fynbos which have remained unburned for 30-65 years, and we have recorded no successful interfire recruitment to reproductive age in *Banksia hookeriana* for stands up to 21 years old. The lack of older sites precludes further direct study of this question. The wastage of scarce resources (i.e. seed loss) in plants older than 22 years might imply that, historically, sites rarely reach this age before fire recurs. In support of this contention, we have been unable to locate any sites containing plants older than 23 years (Enright & Lamont unpublished data). However, this may also reflect a recent increase in fire frequency due to human interference.
226	
227	Diversity and evenness in the canopy seed store modelled here had not peaked by the estimated optimum return time for fire. Nevertheless, diversity (H′) rises only slowly once this optimum is passed and evenness is always high. One possible consequence of dormant seed banks is the presence of seeds produced in different years which might reflect different pollen parents and selective forces (Harper 1977), i.e. it increases genetic diversity of the seed pool. This might help to buffer the species against rapid evolutionary drift, and at the same time increase resilience of the species in the face of fluctuating environmental conditions. These advantages apply to short-lived species characterized by soil seed storage where parent plants represent different generations. The advantages for longer lived, cohort regenerator species such as *Banksia hookeriana* are less obvious, as all or most pollen will derive from neighbours of identical age which were recruited following the same disturbance and have experienced similar growing conditions. Instead, selfing would probably increase with age as flower head production per plant and death of neighbours increased, cancelling out increasing seed age diversity. Cowling (1987) argued that serotinous nonsprouting species (such as *Banksia hookeriana*) are prone to strong selection pressure, particularly at the seedling stage. He considered that the high number of discrete sexual generations, and fragmentation of populations through fire-mediated local extinction, implies a rapid evolutionary rate and may explain the high level of speciation in *Banksia* and other taxa with similar life histories.
228	
229	The recent history of fire within the geographical range of *Banksia hookeriana* suggests shorter intervals between successive fires than we propose as optimal for species' maintenance. A wildfire in January 1984 burned 117 000 ha of the northern sandplain heath (van der Moezel *et al.* 1987), an area equivalent to nearly half of the total geographical range of the species. In the autumn of 1991 wildfire again covered part of the 1984 burn area near Mt Adams, a return period of only 7 years. This fire eliminated *Banksia hookeriana* from one of the plots enumerated here. Van der Moezel *et al.* (1987) comment that areas of sandplain heath vegetation older than 11 years are becoming increasingly scarce since the establishment of farms and roads in the area and a hazard-reduction burning policy for the remaining natural vegetation.

235	Both species took some 2.5 years after the fire to establish seedlings. Other species either cohabiting with *D*. *excelsa* and *T*. *speciosissima*, or from other fire-prone habitats, established seedlings much sooner. In general, those species with a soil seed bank mostly establish seedlings within the first year after a fire, while those with a canopy seed bank mostly release seed in the first 6 months (Lamont and Barker 1988; Lamont *et al.* 1991) and establish seedlings in the first year (Table 5). Even other species that rely on post-fire flowering for seedling establishment appear to be 0.5–1.5 years quicker than *D*. *excelsa* and *T*. *speciosissima* in establishing seedlings post-fire (Table 5). Among other Australian species, Auld (1986) found that for the shrub *Angophora hispida*, establishment occurred within about 18 months, while seedlings of shrubby *Xanthorrhoea* spp. were observed 18 months to 2 years after fire (Benwell 1998; Curtis 1998; Taylor *et al.* 1998). This is also the case in other fire-prone areas of the world, including Californian sage scrub, Florida sand pine scrub and South African fynbos (Table 5). By the time seedlings of *D*. *excelsa* and *T*. *speciosissima* are becoming established, much of the space, light and nutrients made available by the fire may have been captured by other species (both resprouting plants and seedlings). This will be particularly the case for seedlings from the second and third fruit crops post-fire in *T*. *speciosissima*. In other vegetation types, resprouting species may be able to continue recruiting new seedlings several years after fire (e.g. *Garberia heterophylla* in Florida, Abrahamson and Abrahamson 1996). Curtis (1998) observed seedlings of the arborescent monocot, *X*. *australis*, at sites unburnt for about 100 years. However, such inter-fire recruitment has rarely been observed in the post-fire environment of *D*. *excelsa* and *T*. *speciosissima*. Thus, despite the tolerance of their adults to fire, the persistence of these species may in part be due to their large seed size, which ensures that seedlings have sufficient reserves to
236	
237	establish (Westoby *et al.* 1992; Lamont and Groom 1998), although the relative proportions of different nutrients in these seeds has not been determined (Lamont and Groom 1998; Myerscough *et al.* 2000).
238	
239	Primary seed dispersal for both species produced a high concentration of seeds adjacent to the adult and an exponential decay of seed density with distance. This pattern is typical of a broad range of other plant species (Janzen 1970; Auld 1986; Willson 1992; Hammill *et al.* 1998). However, Hammill *et al.* (1998) found that seeds from species with canopy seed banks were dispersed at considerably greater distances than found here for *D*. *excelsa* or *T*. *speciosissima*. Differences in dispersal distances between our study species and between sites for *T*. *speciosissima* in this study are probably related to the height of the infructescences and the height and density of the surrounding vegetation (Hammill *et al.* 1998). Infructescences of *D*. *excelsa* at Site 1 were on average 3.9 m (±0.15 s.e.) tall. For *T*. *speciosissima* at Site 1, infructescences were relatively shorter at 1.85 m (±0.08 s.e.), while *T*. *speciosissima* at Site 3 had the shortest infructescences at 0.95 m (±0.08 s.e.). The surrounding vegetation at Site 3 appeared to be denser than at Site 1 and this may have further contributed to the shorter dispersal distances. Dispersal along the ground by wind or water in heavy rains may also have contributed to these dispersal patterns (Harper 1977; Hammill *et al.* 1998). For serotinous species that release seeds shortly after fire, the understorey would be relatively open at the time of seed release, while for *D*. *excelsa* and *T*. *speciosissima*, considerable post-fire regrowth would have increased the density of the understorey. This may act to limit seed dispersal in *D*. *excelsa* and *T*. *speciosissima*.
240	
241	The exclosure experiment indicated that seed losses to mammals and invertebrates occurred in the field (Fig. 2), as has been found for other large-seeded species in similar habitats (e.g. *Banksia* spp., *Isopogon anemonifolius* and *Petrophile pulchella*, Bradstock 1991; *Protea neriifolia*, Botha and Le Maitre 1992; *Grevillea* spp., Auld and Denham 1999, 2001; *Hakea sericea* and *P*. *pulchella*, R. J. Whelan and J. York*,* unpubl. data). Generally, other studies have found greatly reduced predation in burnt sites (Bradstock 1991; Botha and le Maitre 1992), while R. J. Whelan and J. York (unpubl. data) found that survival of seeds among exclusion treatments was extremely variable among fires and sites. The high level of losses observed in this study is more comparable to that found at unburnt sites (e.g. 100% losses, Bradstock 1991; 75–100% Botha and Le Maitre 1992; 82–95%, Auld and Denham 1999), and to that of recently burnt sites for *Grevillea caleyi* (Auld and Denham 2001). Most seed losses were presumably caused by mammals rather than invertebrates, on the basis of the patterns of seed removal and *in situ* damage. Losses were high for clumped seeds, but generally lower for seeds placed singly, implying that local seed density may affect the ability of seed predators to find 
242	
243	{11}<!-- PAGE BREAK -->
244	
245	and subsequently eat seeds. Differences in seed losses between study species at Site 1 for low-density seeds may reflect a difference in palatability of seeds or degree of predator satiation, given the much greater seed production in *D*. *excelsa* (Table 1). At Site 3 for *T*. *speciosissima*, losses were high for seeds at high and low densities. While predator satiation may occur in the immediate post-fire period when species with canopy seed banks release seeds, it appears that such effects are less important by the time *D*. *excelsa* and *T*. *speciosissima* release seeds. Consequently, if recruitment is not limited by a lack of safe sites, then seed losses to predators are likely to have had an impact on the magnitude of seedling recruitment, particularly for *T*. *speciosissima* at Site 3.
246	
247	Seedling recruitment was observed at all sites, but generally only a small percentage of the seeds released successfully established (≤4%, Table 3). The exception was at Site 1 for *T*. *speciosissima* where about 14% of all seeds released post-fire were established as seedlings. However, seedling densities by 1998 were comparable between *D*. *excelsa* and *T*. *speciosissima* at Site 1 (0.3 per m<sup>2</sup> , Table 3), resulting from the much greater seed production of *D*. *excelsa* at this site (Table 1). In contrast, for *T*. *speciosissima* at Site 3, seedling densities were an order of magnitude lower (0.03 per m<sup>2</sup> , Table 3), even though there was no significant difference in seed production to *T*. *speciosissima* at Site 1.

For *T*. *speciosissima* at Site 1, infructescences were relatively shorter at 1.85 m (±0.08 s.e.), while *T*. *speciosissima* at Site 3 had the shortest infructescences at 0.95 m (±0.08 s.e.). The surrounding vegetation at Site 3 appeared to be denser than at Site 1 and this may have further contributed to the shorter dispersal distances. Dispersal along the ground by wind or water in heavy rains may also have contributed to these dispersal patterns (Harper 1977; Hammill *et al.* 1998). For serotinous species that release seeds shortly after fire, the understorey would be relatively open at the time of seed release, while for *D*. *excelsa* and *T*. *speciosissima*, considerable post-fire regrowth would have increased the density of the understorey. This may act to limit seed dispersal in *D*. *excelsa* and *T*. *speciosissima*.

The exclosure experiment indicated that seed losses to mammals and invertebrates occurred in the field (Fig. 2), as has been found for other large-seeded species in similar habitats (e.g. *Banksia* spp., *Isopogon anemonifolius* and *Petrophile pulchella*, Bradstock 1991; *Protea neriifolia*, Botha and Le Maitre 1992; *Grevillea* spp., Auld and Denham 1999, 2001; *Hakea sericea* and *P*. *pulchella*, R. J. Whelan and J. York*,* unpubl. data). Generally, other studies have found greatly reduced predation in burnt sites (Bradstock 1991; Botha and le Maitre 1992), while R. J. Whelan and J. York (unpubl. data) found that survival of seeds among exclusion treatments was extremely variable among fires and sites. The high level of losses observed in this study is more comparable to that found at unburnt sites (e.g. 100% losses, Bradstock 1991; 75–100% Botha and Le Maitre 1992; 82–95%, Auld and Denham 1999), and to that of recently burnt sites for *Grevillea caleyi* (Auld and Denham 2001). Most seed losses were presumably caused by mammals rather than invertebrates, on the basis of the patterns of seed removal and *in situ* damage. Losses were high for clumped seeds, but generally lower for seeds placed singly, implying that local seed density may affect the ability of seed predators to find 

{11}<!-- PAGE BREAK -->

and subsequently eat seeds. Differences in seed losses between study species at Site 1 for low-density seeds may reflect a difference in palatability of seeds or degree of predator satiation, given the much greater seed production in *D*. *excelsa* (Table 1). At Site 3 for *T*. *speciosissima*, losses were high for seeds at high and low densities. While predator satiation may occur in the immediate post-fire period when species with canopy seed banks release seeds, it appears that such effects are less important by the time *D*. *excelsa* and *T*. *speciosissima* release seeds. Consequently, if recruitment is not limited by a lack of safe sites, then seed losses to predators are likely to have had an impact on the magnitude of seedling recruitment, particularly for *T*. *speciosissima* at Site 3.

Seedling recruitment was observed at all sites, but generally only a small percentage of the seeds released successfully established (≤4%, Table 3). The exception was at Site 1 for *T*. *speciosissima* where about 14% of all seeds released post-fire were established as seedlings. However, seedling densities by 1998 were comparable between *D*. *excelsa* and *T*. *speciosissima* at Site 1 (0.3 per m<sup>2</sup> , Table 3), resulting from the much greater seed production of *D*. *excelsa* at this site (Table 1). In contrast, for *T*. *speciosissima* at Site 3, seedling densities were an order of magnitude lower (0.03 per m<sup>2</sup> , Table 3), even though there was no significant difference in seed production to *T*. *speciosissima* at Site 1.

content.content:
1	# The ecological significance of canopy seed storage in fire-prone environments: a model for non-sprouting shrubs
2	
3	NEAL J. ENRIGHT*†, RALF MARSULA‡, BYRON B. LAMONT† and CHRISTIAN WISSEL‡
4	
5	*Department of Geography and Environmental Studies, University of Melbourne, Parkville 3052, Australia; †School of Environmental Biology, Curtin University of Technology, GPO Box U1987 Perth 6001, Australia; and ‡Department of Ecological Modelling, UFZ Centre for Environmental Research, Leipzig-Halle, Permoserstr. 15, PF 2, D-04301 Leipzig, Germany
6	
7	Correspondence: Dr Neal Enright (fax 61 3 9344 4972; e-mail enright@ariel.ucs.unimelb.edu.au).
8	
9	# Summary
10	
11	1 A comprehensive data set on age, survival and reproduction for the non-sprouting (fire-killed) shrub Banksia hookeriana, encompassing 13 years of measurements at 15 sites in south-western Australia, and including 10 fires, was used to parameterize a computer model to investigate optimum plant life-history strategies in a fire-prone environment. Parameter ranges encompassed life-history information for other non-sprouting Banksia species from the same region.
12	
13	2 The relationship between fire interval and level of canopy seed storage (serotiny) was analysed to identify the circumstances under which serotiny is favoured, and what degree of serotiny maximizes potential population growth rate. In addition to deterministic versions of the model, stochasticity in fire interval and conditions for recruitment were analysed.
14	
15	3 The deterministic model indicated a maximum finite rate of natural increase (λ = 1.15) when the fire interval was 16 years and all seeds were retained on the plant until fire occurred. Although the model failed to predict the intermediate degrees of serotiny present in nature, it supported the optimum fire interval predicted from canopy seed bank dynamics.
16	
17	4 Changes to biological attributes associated with timing of reproduction and longevity shifted the optimum fire interval and estimated rate of population growth, but did not alter the conclusions concerning serotiny. Although shorter seed longevity and increased rates of predation and/or decay reduced the value of serotiny, even very low levels of canopy seed storage increased species fitness under intermediate fire frequencies (10–20 years).
18	
19	5 If the probability of inter-fire recruitment and survival was increased, optimum growth shifted from strong serotiny under a regime of frequent fire (<20 year interval), to weak (or no) serotiny where the interval between successive fires was long (>40 year interval).
20	
21	6 Stochasticity around mean fire interval resulted in intermediate to strong (but not complete) serotiny being predicted as optimal once the CV for fire interval approached 100%. This result is interpreted as a bet-hedging strategy whereby spontaneous release of some seeds during the inter-fire period permits recruitment on rare occasions where fire interval approaches or exceeds the species longevity.
22	
23	Keywords: Banksia, computer models, fire regime, optimum life-history strategies, serotiny, stochastic effects, woody plants
24	
25	Journal of Ecology (1998) 86, 946–959
26	
27	<!-- PAGE BREAK -->
28	
29	# Introduction
30	
31	Plants in fire-prone environments are often characterized by biological attributes that increase the probability of survival and/or recruitment following disturbance by fire. Among these are the ability of individuals to regrow from protected buds either above- or below-ground (resprouting), fire-stimulated flowering and seed production, and fire-triggered germination of seeds stored either in the soil or in the plant canopy (Gill 1981). Since species that resprout after fire commonly co-exist in fire-prone environments (e.g. mediterranean-type shrublands) with those that are killed by fire (non-sprouters), a frequent question concerns the circumstances under which one or other strategy is favoured (e.g. Keeley & Zedler 1978; Keeley 1986; Hilbert 1987). Beyond this simple dichotomous division into resprouters and non-sprouters, fire-prone communities may contain an array of (sometimes congeneric) species showing consistent variation in the amount of resprouting after fire, the extent to which seeds are stored in the soil or on the plant, and in other biological attributes (e.g. longevity, age to reproduction, level of seed production).
32	
33	It is important to determine the biological attributes that influence demographic behaviour and to establish which attributes confer the greatest fitness advantage on a species in relation to particular fire regimes. As well as revealing information on the selective pressures acting on species in fire-prone environments, the answers aid conservation and management of species in relation to human-imposed fire regimes.
34	
35	This paper presents a computer model of population dynamics for a non-sprouting woody perennial in a fire-prone environment, and the results of simulations which sought to reveal the optimum level of on-plant seed storage (serotiny) in relation to fire interval. Serotiny refers to the retention of seeds in closed fruits or cones within the crown for more than 1 year and is common in species from a number of important families in fire-prone areas of Australia (Proteaceae, Myrtaceae, Cupressaceae, Casuarinaceae), South Africa (Proteaceae, Bruniaceae) and North America (Pinaceae) (Lamont et al. 1991a). It can be contrasted with two alternative fates of seeds: storage in a soil seed bank, or release of short-lived seeds once mature (no seed storage). Seed release in serotinous species is normally triggered by fire and seeds are short-lived after release, germinating during the first favourable period (Cowling & Lamont 1987). Species can range from weakly serotinous, where most seeds are released spontaneously (in the absence of fire) within a few years of production, to strongly serotinous, where most seeds are held in the canopy for many years (e.g. >10 years in some species of Pinus and Banksia).
36	
37	The ecological and evolutionary significance of serotiny seems clear: where fire is the most common cause of ecosystem disturbance, cued release of canopy-stored seeds by fire (and their germination in the first growing season after fire) maximizes plant age and therefore seed available for the next generation by the time of the next fire. Seeds released, and seedlings established, later during the inter-fire period have a lower probability of survival due to competition with their parents and other established plants (Cowling & Lamont 1987). They will be younger and will thus have a smaller canopy seed bank when fire recurs, and so are less fit (sensu Stearns 1992). It would therefore appear that very strong serotiny should represent the optimum strategy for perennial plants in fire-prone environments. However, a range of degrees of serotiny may be encountered within the same plant community (e.g. Cowling et al. 1987; Enright & Lamont 1989a,b) or even within the same species. In the latter case, variations have been found in relation to environmental gradients, e.g. lower serotiny in less fire-prone parts of the species' geographical range for Banksia attenuata in Australia (Cowling & Lamont 1985), and in relation to time since last fire, e.g. inter-fire recruits show lower serotiny than immediate post-fire recruits of Pinus banksiana in boreal forests of southern Quebec (Gautier et al. 1996). Lamont et al. (1991a) note that some fire regimes and growth forms apparently foster incomplete serotiny, but that 'degree of serotiny has received little formal treatment, and the empirical subtleties of such relationships remain largely unexplored'.
38	
39	The model described here is based on field data collected over 13 years from 15 sites and including 10 different fires (up to two at the same site) for B. hookeriana Meissn. (Proteaceae), a non-sprouting woody shrub of mediterranean-type shrublands in south-western Australia (Enright & Lamont 1989a, 1992a,b; Enright et al. 1996). Nevertheless, the model is likely to have a more general application since parameter values can readily be changed to match the known life-history attributes of other serotinous, non-sprouting perennial plants. By basing the model and its parameter values on those measured over an extended period of time (and at a number of sites) for a real plant species the model described here avoids many of the criticisms levelled at population models. For example, Cousens (1995) argues that the results of simulation studies for hypothetical species are often determined largely by the structure of the models themselves and provide little insight into real population dynamic behaviour and, further, that many models based on real data are flawed since the data are derived from glasshouse experiments or from density studies that exclude stochastic year-to-year variations in factors unrelated to density (e.g. weather).
40	
41	<!-- PAGE BREAK -->
42	
43	# Ecological and biological attributes of B. hookeriana
44	
45	### FIELD DATA COLLECTION
46	
47	Banksia hookeriana is a highly serotinous, fire-killed (non-sprouting) woody shrub that grows up to 2.5 m in height, which is restricted to the northern sandplain heaths of south-western Australia (centred on 29°30′S, 115°15′E) about 250–330 km north of Perth (George 1981; Taylor & Hopper 1988). Seed production and plant survivorship were estimated for sample populations of different ages (i.e. time since last fire). Sites covering the whole range of possible plant ages could not be located, and fires during the course of remeasurements returned some sites to zero age. Fifteen sample plots, each 400 m² in area, and ranging in age from 1 to 16 years at the start of the study, were established and censused annually in June (i.e. at the end of the summer–autumn period of peak plant mortality) from 1986 to 1996.
48	
49	The onset and level of flowering (inflorescence) and cone (infructescence) production were recorded for all individuals within five replicate 25 m² subplots per plot for stands <8 years old, and annual cone production followed for a random sample of 10 individuals for older stands. Fertile cones typically carry 5–15 woody follicles arranged around a central rachis, each follicle holding two seeds. Cones arise terminally at the beginning of each growing season, and node scars and branching pattern clearly mark the boundary between successive years of vegetative growth. Thus plant age and individual cone age can be determined with only a small likelihood of error. Complete cone crops were harvested from 20 randomly chosen 16-year-old plants in 1986, and cones were aged so that the entire history of reproduction could be determined for each plant. The numbers of firm, aborted, eaten and decayed seeds in closed follicles were determined by cone age, and viability of firm seeds was assessed by germination testing (full details are provided in Enright et al. 1996). Degree of serotiny was based on the proportion of follicles per cone age class that remained closed in the absence of fire (following Lamont et al. 1991a).
50	
51	The total number of cones per plant was quantified for all plants in plots affected by wild fires during the course of the field study. The number of follicles opened by fire was enumerated for a random sample of 10 cones on each of 10 plant skeletons per plot, and the number of viable seeds released per plant estimated using data for seeds from harvested cones.
52	
53	Plant survivorship was recorded annually for 10 randomly chosen individuals within each subplot where plant age was <8 years, and in the whole plot for older stands. The number of seeds released following fire, the number of seedlings established in the first winter, and number of survivors at each age was used to produce survivorship trajectories. These trajectories described the number of seeds required to produce a new individual of any particular age.
54	
55	Data for three other non-sprouting Banksia species (B. prionotes Lindley, B. leptophylla A.S. George and B. lanata A.S. George) provided information on ranges for parameter values for modelling purposes. Up to six Banksia species (a mixture of resprouters and non-sprouters) co-occurred in some of the field sites. The biological attributes of these species are described in Cowling et al. (1987), Enright & Lamont (1989a) and Enright & Lamont (1992a).
56	
57	### SPECIES ATTRIBUTES
58	
59	Seed production typically commences when plants are 5 years old and fluctuates widely around a mean of about 200 viable seeds per year from 15 years onwards (Enright et al. 1996). While new inflorescences may be damaged and removed from plants by birds, mature cones normally remain attached to the plant throughout their life. Few seeds are released except when fire causes the follicles on cones to open. Once released, seeds either germinate with the onset of winter rains or perish (Enright & Lamont 1989a). Enright et al. (1996) describe in detail the mean rate of accumulation of viable seeds in the canopy in relation to plant age. On average, 17% of embryos abort; seed losses due to spontaneous release in the absence of fire average 4% per annum; while predation and decay of seeds stored in closed follicles increases by 4% per annum from the first year.
60	
61	From 3% to 27% of seeds released following fires in the period 1985–93 produced seedlings in the first winter (Enright & Lamont 1989a; N. J. Enright, unpublished data). Plant survivorship is lowest in the first year and quickly increases such that there is little mortality (<1% year⁻¹) in plants older than 8 years. While no plants older than 25 years have been observed in the field, the continuing survival of most individuals in our oldest study site (N. J. Enright, unpublished data) indicates that longevity may be 30–40 years in the absence of fire. Large, old plants may succumb to drought over summer, and are prone to collapse due to the heavy load of seed-bearing cones on old branches, and this suggests an increased mortality rate for old plants.
62	
63	In the absence of fire, some seeds are released by the spontaneous opening of old fruits, but the probability of germination and survival of recruits to reproductive age is extremely low. Seedlings are occasionally encountered in stands >15 years old, but so far no such recruits have been recorded to survive to reproductive age. Nevertheless, it is reasonable to assume that occasionally these inter-fire recruits might grow to maturity and contribute to future generations. The low chance of establishment, combined with low rates of seed release when the degree of serotiny is high, means that very few recruits are likely via this pathway.
64	
65	<!-- PAGE BREAK -->
66	
67	Seed release is hastened by the death of stem tissues due to drought stress and plant senescence, but is incomplete relative to seed release after fire (Witkowski et al. 1991). The canopy seed bank may be completely lost where plant death occurs before the next fire, both because even if seeds are released they will have a low probability of establishment, and because dead plants are usually completely incinerated by fire so that any seeds still held in the crown will perish (Lamont & Barker 1988). The woody stems and cones on living shrubs burn less intensely due to a higher moisture content, and although the stems are killed they remain standing and the cones are opened but not consumed. If fire occurs either before the onset of reproductive maturity, or before a sufficient canopy seed bank has accumulated, a population is threatened with local extinction.
68	
69	### WEATHER AND FIRE
70	
71	Mediterranean-type climate regions are characterized by cool, moist winters and hot, dry summers. In the northern sandplain heaths of south-western Australia, winter rains are highly predictable and will almost always provide sufficient moisture to allow seedling establishment after fire. However, the extent of summer drought is more variable. One-hundred and ten years of rainfall records for nearby Dongara (Western Australian Bureau of Meteorology climate station 8044; 29°15′S, 114°56′E, mean annual rainfall of 471 mm for the period 1884–1993) show that about 80% of summers have the typical mediterranean-type pattern of low to very low rainfall. In the other 20% of years, tropical storms punctuate the summer with heavy rainfall events and drought stress on plants is greatly reduced (Enright & Lamont 1992a).
72	
73	Summer weather conditions are important in determining levels of seedling survival in the first year following fire. Survivorship of seedlings is highest in wet summers and lowest in dry summers (Enright & Lamont 1992a). There was no relationship between rainfall in the previous summer and subsequent inflorescence production for plants >15 years old. However, there was a significant positive relationship between total rainfall in one year and inflorescence production in the next (log10 cones = 5.45 × log10 annual rainfall – 13.80; d.f. = 16, F = 10.50, P < 0.05, r² = 0.36). This non-linear relationship suggests reduced inflorescence production following years of lower than average rainfall, but little increase above average levels of production following wet years.
74	
75	Risk of fire is high every summer and there is no obvious relationship between rainfall and fire: of nine wild fires recorded in the vicinity of the field area since 1967, four occurred in wetter than average years, and four in years with very dry summers (one of which followed a wet winter). However, the timing of fire in relation to rainfall in the first few years after fire (especially unusually wet or dry summers) is important since seedling mortality is highest during this period (Enright & Lamont 1989a, 1992a). Stands burned within the last 5 years are unlikely to have accumulated sufficient biomass to carry a fire. The shortest recorded fire interval in relation to the nine fires noted above was 7 years.
76	
77	# Methods
78	
79	### THE MODEL
80	
81	The computer model, written in C++, describes the population dynamics of a serotinous, non-sprouting woody perennial that is subject to disturbance by fire. We chose an age-based approach to characterize the population: the model traces the number of x-year-old plants, N(x), and the number of seeds stored on an x-year-old plant, S(x), for each age x. Changes in N(x) and S(x) are caused by plant death, seed production, seed loss, seed release, germination and establishment of seedlings. These processes are described by the functional relationships detailed below, and illustrated conceptually in Fig. 1. The model begins with a post-fire population of 100 viable seeds and calculates their survivorship and reproduction in relation to age until fire causes plant death and seed release. Fire kills all individuals, and recruitment following fire is solely from seeds.
82	
83	Germination, establishment and survivorship of plants depend on the growing conditions (especially summer rainfall), and the model uses the fits derived from field data on survivorship, and illustrated in Fig. 2, to describe these rates. The probability of germination of seeds and establishment of seedlings in the first year is the inverse of the observed number of seeds required for self-replacement of a 1-year-old plant. In the same way, the probability p(x) that a plant survives until it is x years old is the inverse of the number of seeds required for self-replacement of a plant at age x. Thus, the probability p(x, x + 1) to survive from year x to year x + 1 can be calculated
84	
85	Fig. 1 Summary flow diagram of the main processes built into the computer model for a serotinous, non-sprouting perennial plant. Note this is not a complete flow diagram of the model. Full model details are described in the text.
86	
87	<!-- PAGE BREAK -->
88	
89	Fig. 2 The mean number of viable seeds required to produce a new plant of given age, over plant ages 0–10 years, for B. hookeriana, and the best-fit regression lines describing (a) good, (b) average, (c) bad and (d) very bad recruitment, respectively. Regression model details in the text.
90	
91	as the ratio p (x, x + 1) = p (x + 1)/p (x). The best fit regression line describing recruitment under average conditions is: number of viable seeds required per recruit = 69.03 × log(age) + 23.60) (d.f. = 1,72, F = 39.1, P < 0.001). Other functions are: in good weather, number of viable seeds = 26.54 × log (age) + 23.03; in bad weather, number of viable seeds = 116.53 × log(age) + 82.16; and, in very bad weather, number of viable seeds = 451.72 × log (age) + 17.67. These fits encompass a broader range of measured field recruitment responses than would be the case if regression model (95% or 99%) confidence limits were used to define good and bad recruitment, and are argued to reflect more realistically the natural variation in recruitment in relation to variation in summer rainfall. The impacts that climate have on population growth rate are based on the classification of post-fire years as good (>40 mm summer rainfall), average (10–40 mm), bad (1–10 mm) and very bad (0 mm).
92	
93	At each time step the plants get 1 year older. The model calculates the age class distribution of the individuals as well as their seed production in that year and accumulated seed storage in the plant canopy. Plants have an increased risk of mortality once an age of 25 years is exceeded. This mortality rate increases from 0 to 0.1 by steps of 0.01 per year such that <20% of plants alive at age 25 years are still alive at age 40 years. Maximum plant longevity is described by the parameter A4 (Table 1).
94	
95	Juvenile plants commence seed production at plant age A2 years. Seed production increases linearly up to age A3, after which it remains constant at Fm seeds per year. Most seeds are stored in the plant canopy, but the seeds in a proportion, Lv, of follicles are lost each year due to predation and rotting, while a further proportion, r, open each year in the absence of fire and release their seeds (inter-fire release). 1/r (the inverse of r) describes the degree of serotiny. Thus, a value of 1 for serotiny means that all seeds are released by the end of the year in which they were produced (i.e. the plant is not serotinous), while a value of 1000 means that, on average, only 0.1% of the seed crop is released per year and nearly all of the seed crop (regardless of seed age) is held on the plant until fire triggers seed release. This definition of serotiny follows that proposed by Lamont (1991). The degree of serotiny can theoretically range from 1 (0% serotiny) to infinity (100% serotiny) but most recorded values (e.g. for Banksia species) fall between 10 and 100 (Table 2).
96	
97	Seeds have a longevity of Vm years on the plant. Seeds released during the inter-fire period have a lower probability of germination and establishment than seeds released in response to fire (post-fire release). 181	### DETERMINISTIC ANALYSES
182	
183	Deterministic analysis with parameters set to those for B. hookeriana reveals a broad peak in the estimated finite rate of natural increase (λ) for fire intervals of 12–25 years, with a maximum (λ = 1.15) at 16 years (Fig. 3a). λ increases with degree of serotiny to a peak at maximum serotiny (i.e. 1000; no seeds released except as caused by fire), with the rate of increase in λ greatest as degree of serotiny rises from 1 to 10. That is, although fitness is maximized for complete serotiny, the advantages of serotiny over non-serotiny are quickly realized with any tendency towards prolonged on-plant seed storage. Population decline (extinction) is predicted at very short fire intervals, with the risk of extinction greater for non-serotinous (intervals ⩽11 years), than for highly serotinous (intervals ⩽8 years), plants. At very long fire intervals (>40 years) extreme serotiny is a disadvantage.

Extinction is predicted where fire occurs before the plants reach reproductive age or when they have not had time to accumulate a sufficient canopy seed store to ensure successful recruits following fire: this point is frequently made in the fire ecology literature (e.g. Gill 1981; Lamont et al. 1991a). A fire interval in excess of 40 years also leads to extinction if degree of serotiny is close to 1000, since the longevity of plants is exceeded and few or no seeds have been released prior to plant death. This result is consistent with the findings of Bond (1980), who documented the decline of serotinous Proteaceae populations in South African fynbos that had remained unburned for 30–65 years.
